As my colleague said, it is going to be chaired by the Deputy Speaker and, with that, it’s also going to have equal membership between Government and Opposition party members, just to ensure that whatever does happen within the legislative scrutiny committee is able to have the same transparency but, also, the same robustness as what we do here in this particular House.
: I note that the legislative scrutiny committee could take part in or replace what is considered the select committee stage between the first and second readings,  as well as, for some bills, even committee of the whole House, between the second and third readings, with the approval of the Business Committee. I think that’s really important, when we’re looking at how that is going to be working in practice—ensuring a level of oversight by the Business Committee.
: It was mentioned previously, I think, by the Leader of the House that there are some elements in the report around the use of artificial intelligence (AI). This is something that we are approaching in an incredibly cautious way with how AI can be or could be used in terms of looking at some of the submissions. I think one of the things that the committee and the report is very clear on is to ensure that there is still a high degree of oversight in terms of how and when that could be used, and the committee must still be asked permission in order to undertake that, noting that we have seen in select committees a significant increase in submissions in this term of Parliament, particularly on the Justice Committee. With this, there has been some allowance that has been given in the analysis—or the expediency when it comes to analysis—of some of the submissions. Again, this is something that I think is important and prudent for the 55th Parliament and the future Standing Orders Committee and select committees in general to keep an eye on.
: A couple of other things I want to touch on is, number one, some of the changes to the omnibus bill and some of the changes to the way that we look at minor updates. This is specifically to Standing Order 267. I think it’s also an important ability for any Government to be able to include more minor amendments or the allowance to have more minor amendments—again, pending the approval from Business Committee—incorporated as part of an omnibus bill, particularly when minor amendments affect more than two principal Acts.
: Something that’s very important to me and very dear to me is some of the adjustments to international treaty examinations in Standing Order 405. The reason I say that is because, currently, as part of our dualist system, international treaties can be signed up to by any Government and that includes trade agreements, and then it goes through a trade examination process by the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee. But then the agreement has already been signed, and there’s very little ability to truly really examine the agreement when any Government has already signed up to the agreement. Of course, it only becomes domestic legislation if there is an ensuing domestic law. While we didn’t get everything we want to see in terms of, I guess, the specific ability for Parliament to scrutinise any executive branch of the Government around international treaty examination, the review does allow the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee greater power in conducting some of those analyses, including some of the abilities to have briefings, etc.
: Finally, in terms of the ongoing tidy-ups of how we now conduct the financial scrutiny with the introduction of scrutiny weeks under this Parliament, I do want to thank our previous Green Party MP, Jan Logie, for some of the work that she has done in getting this new system up and running. It’s something that we are continuously improving on. With that, we commend the report to the House.
TODD STEPHENSON (ACT): Thank you, Mr Speaker. Look, I rise to speak on the review of Standing Orders. Again, just like my colleagues across the House, I want to thank you, Mr Speaker, for chairing the Standing Orders Committee, and to the Clerk of the House and his team. It’s not a very easy task to get consensus across all of the different political parties, but that’s exactly what we did do in these in this Standing Orders review. I think it was a great process, taking the time—and I think you commented, Mr Speaker, that we started a bit earlier in this Parliament, so we took a bit more time to get to work through the different issues, which was good.
: I also want to thank, actually, submitters. This is just like any other select committee, where submitters were able to make submissions on the Standing Orders. I just want to thank the people that took the time to do that. They’re actually set out in Appendix C of the report, so if you want to have a look, you can.
: I’m just going to use my time to talk about a couple of areas which I think were really useful. I want to suggest to incoming MPs that they actually take the time to read the report in the new Parliament, because that’s where it’s going to be most useful. We did spend quite a lot of time on select committees and, actually, in the report, it talks about what is the purpose of a select committee. I think a lot of discussion has been because of the large number of submissions that a lot of select committees, including the Justice Committee, got in this Parliament. We’re actually outlining, now, in the Standing Orders what is the purpose of the select committee process. Again, it really is to try and result in high-quality legislation.
: So it’s really providing—and, again, that’s why it’d be important for MPs in the next Parliament to read this: it provides a bit of an outline as to what is the objective of the select committee process so that when select committees are going through legislation and getting submissions and deciding who’s going to submit, they can say, “Well, are the submitters we’re going to be hearing from actually going to help us deliver high-quality legislation—yes or no—or are there other reasons?” So, again, just to say you don’t actually have to hear from every submitter and actually think about the value of the submissions on a particular bill and what it might add. I think there’s some really good material in the report around that; making sure that when you are hearing from submitters, it’s actually aligned to that purpose. Again, I think that’s going to be useful for the next select committee members.
: The other one, and Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan talked about this is, is just talking about some issues around omnibus bills, but particularly regulatory systems bills. We saw quite a few of those in this Parliament, as we’ve seen in other Parliaments, but they’re being now specifically called out as a type of omnibus bill that can be used. They are really important bills, regulatory systems bills, because they do keep our statute book up to date. I think that was a really good discussion.
: The other one, again, is around scrutiny week. This is the first Parliament that has had two weeks set aside for different types of scrutiny. I don’t have anything to compare it with, because it’s my first term, but, again, I think just acknowledging some of the learnings from this Parliament around scrutiny weeks—what can be improved or done differently. That provides some really good guidance for select committees.
: The only other two things I’m going to call out were just around petitions. We actually had a sessional order in this Parliament around highly discriminatory content in petitions to Parliament. We don’t want to be hosting or allowing petitions that do have highly discriminatory content, so we had a sessional order, which has now been put into Standing Orders. I think that process we worked really well, and I want to thank both the Clerk and the Petitions Committee for bringing that process to us, and seeing how that worked and how that’s now being put into Standing Orders.
: Finally, I just want to draw people’s attention to Appendix B, which is a really helpful table which talks about Parliament’s workload. You can actually look, over quite a number of Parliaments—I think we’ve got seven set out there—at the number of hours we’ve spent on sittings, different extended hours, committee of the whole House, petitions; everything. It’s a really good resource. You can actually see how this Parliament has compared to others: the number of bills—everything. Again, I think that’s a really useful piece of the report, and I think it’ll be used by people. So, with that, obviously, I want to commend this to the House. Thank you.
JAMIE ARBUCKLE (NZ First): Thank you, Mr Speaker. I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to support the review of the Standing Orders 2026 carried out by the Standing Orders Committee.
: Obviously, we’ve got a number of recommendations in front of us today. Some of those I will touch on briefly, but, firstly, I just thank you for your leadership, for chairing the committee, for your wise words as we went through a number of different submissions on different issues; to the Office of the Clerk and to Dr David Wilson for your reports, that were always timely and very well informed. Obviously, transitioning now from the 54th Parliament, what we’re sitting in today, into the 55th Parliament, my reflection with the Standing Orders is that this is something that has, over many Parliaments, been refined, and what we’re doing here is just, as the Leader of the House did mention, making this a better process, making this place a better place for the 55th Parliament. As we did see last week, there are still times where we get caught off guard, when we were in urgency last week, and there’s going to be continual need to refine these Standing Orders every Parliament. It is something that we just keep refining as we go forward.
: The select committee, if we go back, actually first sat on 30 July 2025, so it has been a very long process, but starting early has been able to give us, I think, a better result than trying to put it into such a short period of time. We received 86 submissions, we received 27 oral submissions to the select committee, and the report back also takes into account the three petitions that the select committee had in front of it.
: The most major change in front of us to the House is the Legislative Scrutiny Committee. That’s something that is going to be new for the 55th Parliament. From all parties involved, we’ve come to the conclusion that that is the best thing to trial in the 55th Parliament. It is there for those non-controversial bills, stuff that otherwise might not be prioritised, and pieces of legislation that Parliament struggles to get to with the workload that we do have. This Legislative Scrutiny Committee no doubt will need some refining. It is something new, but I think we all struggle in this House, from time to time, with some of the processes through the committee of the whole House, the hours that are spent, often on legislation that we all agree on. This opportunity to trial this new Legislative Scrutiny Committee is, I think, something that will see a lot more legislation passed but also the more important pieces of legislation actually debated in this Chamber.
: Also, around the scrutiny weeks, there is some clarity around Estimates and making sure that Ministers are available around Estimates—not so much around the annual reviews—and also that question in scrutiny weeks of making sure that the business that is conducted in those weeks is actually scrutiny and not other business in front of the committee.
: An important part, also, was the select committee having a purpose statement. That purpose statement—I think it’s on page 17—actually sets out that the primary purpose of considering a bill is to ensure that, if the bill is passed, it results in high-quality legislation. Why I bring that to the attention of the House is that we’ve received a massive amount of submissions on bills in this term of Parliament. I think it’s, like, 700,000 submissions; 39 bills have attracted over 1,000 submissions. What that actually relates to is, in the past 30 years of the House sitting with legislation, 1.4 million submissions in 30 years, but 700,000 of those have been in this term of Parliament. With the amount of submissions being received through select committee, having a purpose statement—it is not practical any more to hear from everybody, but it is actually making that quality of legislation.
: One part important to New Zealand First, that we did comment on through a submission, was members’ attire—how members actually present themselves in this House. There is a statement here, and something that you did circulate, Mr Speaker, during this term of Parliament, about how the expectation is, obviously, set by the whips and, obviously, our leaders, but, importantly, in the Standing Orders now it does include that men must wear jackets, women must have covered shoulders, T-shirts are not acceptable, and clothing that conveys a graphic or message is not acceptable. I think that, from New Zealand First’s point of view, we’d probably like to see something a little bit stronger, but it is in the right direction.
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins: Winston likes things that are a bit stronger.
JAMIE ARBUCKLE: The other thing—thank you, Chris, for that. The other part to that is, on page 147, what was alluded to by the last speaker, Todd Stephenson: the combined statistics, and the work that this Parliament has done was up to something like 1,773 hours of Parliament’s time, counting the committee of the whole House time. It’s the busiest Parliament that there has ever been, so those statistics going forward are only going to increase, and the numbers that are included there are only up to 11 September. Obviously, with the urgency debates last week, that time frame will push well over 1,800 hours.
: On all that, it was really a pleasure to be part of that select committee—learnt a lot—and I commend the report to the House.
SPEAKER: Before I put the question, I just want to put on record thanks to Dr David Wilson for being so generous with his time and guidance to members, but also to David Bagnall, who was a key adviser to that committee, for his work. This report is the result of a very collaborative process, and I have no problem saying that the question is that the motion be agreed to.
: Motion agreed to.

topicSummaries.topic: Sittings of the House — Adjournment Debate
topicSummaries.content:
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON (Prime Minister): I move, That the House do now adjourn until 2 October 2026.
: Mr Speaker, let me begin by thanking you and your wise leadership of this House, and also, to everyone who has kept this place working over the term: the cleaners, our Copperfields staff, the messengers, Hansard, VIP drivers, the Dignitary Protection Service, security, Parliamentary Counsel Office, the library, IST, select committee staff, finance, travel, reception, building staff, the Cabinet Office, our sign language interpreters, the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, electorate office staff, private secretaries, and everyone in our offices who makes it possible for us to do our work here, can we say thank you, thank you, thank you.
: Can I thank our coalition partners: to David Seymour and to Winston Peters, to all of our colleagues across ACT and New Zealand First, thank you for all of your work this term. Despite every prediction, we have delivered strong and stable government at the moment New Zealanders needed it most. We have shown that three parties can disagree honestly and still work together for New Zealand; we have found common ground, and we have governed in the national interest.
: I do want to pay a special tribute to my National Party colleagues, because they are working away in select committees, late night sittings in urgency, making sure that the promises we made to Kiwis make it through this House. The long hours here away from their families, the long hours back at home solving problems for their constituents, showing up at the school galas and also the public meetings.
: A few thankyous for the other side, too. Can I just thank Willie Jackson for his absolutely outstanding services to the National Party this term? Can I thank Ayesha Verrall, whose relaxed and easy going nature has brought such levity to this Chamber? And can I wish Chris Hipkins all the very best with his now four-year attempt at “just getting warmed up”? I have to say, if that’s him getting warmed up, I’d hate to see him having a lie down!
: I’m incredibly proud of what this Government has achieved. Let’s start with the economy, because three years ago, New Zealand was in trouble. Under Labour, spending grew at one of the fastest rates in our history. Debt tripled, from $60 billion to $180 billion, and it doubled as a share of GDP. For all those billions and all that extra spending and debt, we didn’t get better schools; we didn’t get safer streets or shorter hospital queues. What we got was inflation at a 32-year high, we got food prices up 12 percent, we got higher interest rates, and we got a massive debt bill that’s loaded up on our kids and our grandkids. That is the Labour formula: it is simply spend more, tax more, borrow more. It didn’t work then, but they want to do it all again if they get in.
: Now, on this side, we are getting the books in order. We are stopping a billion dollars that was spent on consultants and contractors. We have halved the price of a new classroom. We are cutting the waste. That means that we can invest more in front-line services. You’re seeing that in health and education. We can invest in those services with no new taxes. We are growing the economy, and growth means jobs, and it means higher incomes. When Todd McClay set out to land a free-trade agreement with India this term, people said it couldn’t be done, but we did it. That means real opportunity, and it means prosperity for all Kiwis across New Zealand. When Chris Bishop set out to fix the Resource Management Act, people said it couldn’t be done, but we did it. That means that this country can now crack on and get things built and get things done. When we promised tax relief, we did it. Nicola Willis delivered the first tax relief in 14 years, because we believe the best place for a Kiwi’s hard-earned dollar is in their back pocket, not sitting over there with Chris Hipkins to waste as he did.
: Let me set the record straight for just one last time, please. Is National considering a capital gains tax?
Hon Members: No.
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: Are we considering a land tax on your farm?
Hon Members: No.
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: What about scrapping Investment Boost?
Hon Members: No.
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: An inheritance tax?
Hon Members: No.
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: A new 45 percent top income tax rate?
Hon Members: No.
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: And what about bringing back Labour’s rental tax?
Hon Members: No.
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: Good. Well, Labour and their mates are lining up nine new taxes, to cover off $18 billion of election freebies. And what’s our answer? Our answer on this side is: no new taxes.
: Well, I’ve got to tell you, New Zealand is heading in the right direction. We have 22 months of manufacturing growth; record exports, up $20 billion; tourism back above pre-COVID levels; first-home buyers are actually a record share of the market, at 29 percent; rent rises are their lowest in 25 years; more Kiwis are choosing to come home for good. In fact, the ones from Australia are up 14 percent; the ones from around the rest of the world up 7 percent. Most importantly, growth is outstripping Australia, the UK, the US, EU, Canada, and Japan. We know it’s been a hard few years, but this is a resilient country that knows, if we stick to the plan, our best days are ahead of us.
: Labour had exactly one law-and-order goal when they were in power, and that was to cut the prison population, irrespective of what was happening on the streets and with crime. I have to say we’ve learnt that “soft on crime” doesn’t work, because violent crime went up 33 percent, retail crime doubled, ram raids quadrupled—all under a Labour Government. So what did Mark Mitchell and Paul Goldsmith do? They put three-strikes together, tougher sentences, and more police on the beat. They banned the gang patches; a new anti-stalking law, and real action on retail crime. Wouldn’t you know it, when you stop making excuses for offenders and you get on the side of victims and start enforcing the law, it actually works! We’ve got 37,000 fewer victims of serious violent crime, serious youth crime is down 26 percent, the ram raids are down 85 percent, and the police out there on the beat doubled, which is fantastic. Incredibly, one of the parties that Chris Hipkins wants to govern with has on their website, “If you’re not trying to abolish prisons, what are you doing in Parliament?” I’ve got to say, well, National is unapologetically backing our police and victims, not the criminals and not the offenders.
: Now, Chris Hipkins was the Minister of Education for five years, and I have to say the record is utterly, utterly shameful. In a First World country, only 46 percent of our kids attended school regularly; 47 percent, by the time they got the high school, were at the standard they needed to be in reading; and, sadly, at high school, only 23 percent were at the standard that they were needing to be at in mathematics. I’ve got to say, Erica Stanford, on the other hand, is doing an excellent job, because she is teaching our kids the basics brilliantly: an hour each of reading, writing, and maths; phones out of the classroom; a brand-new Curriculum; structured literacy; structured numeracy; a relentless focus on attendance; and the biggest investment in learning support in a generation. What are the results: 176,000 kids back at regular school attendance; kids making 12 months’ progress in mathematics in 12 weeks.
: I think one of the worst things that Chris Hipkins did was he scrapped the health targets. Instead, Labour focused on a Māori Health Authority and reorganising the district health boards—not on improving outcomes for patients. The result was longer stays in emergency departments (EDs), longer waits for surgeries, slower cancer treatment. Well, Simeon Brown, and Shane Reti before him—they are turning that around. We have brought back the targets. We’ve invested a record $34 billion in health this year. We’ve boosted doctor training. We’re building a Waikato medical school. We’ve funded 66 new medicines—33 for cancer. And we’ve delivered 51,000 elective surgeries in a single three-month window. As we saw today, it is working: shorter ED wait times, faster elective surgery, faster cancer treatment, higher immunisation rates, and shorter waits for a first specialist assessment.
: New Zealanders have been knocked around by COVID, by lockdowns, by inflation, by Trump’s tariffs, by war in Iran, but things are turning around. We know, in the National Party, that this is the greatest country on Earth, with extraordinary potential still to realise if we make the right choice. This election is a very straight choice: a National Party growing the economy so Kiwis can get ahead, or a radical—a radical—Labour coalition addicted to spending and taxing and borrowing. The choice is poverty or prosperity; chaos or competency; nine new taxes or no new taxes. Be under no illusion, a Labour coalition is going to tax every single ounce of aspiration out of the people trying to leave the next generation better. That is not a New Zealand that we believe in in the National Party. In 45 days, I’ve got to tell you, New Zealanders are going to get a choice, and it’s going to be on our record and on who has the better plan. Make no mistake: this is a policy election.
: A party vote for National will deliver economic growth, new jobs, higher wages, tougher consequences for criminals, more police out on the beat, more trade deals, better school results, replacing NCEA and teaching the basics brilliantly, 30 weeks of paid parental leave, better infrastructure, roads of national significance, new classrooms and new and upgraded hospitals, 5 percent deposits for first-home buyers, universal KiwiSaver, higher contributions, and a $1,500 baby boost, and, most importantly, no new taxes. Yes, there’s more to do, but we are building a future for New Zealand where hard work is rewarded and families can get ahead. There is no time to waste. Our best years are ahead. Bring it on; party vote National.
Rt Hon CHRIS HIPKINS (Leader of the Opposition): Traditionally, a Prime Minister’s speech in the adjournment debate is light-hearted and contains some humour. I was worried when Christopher Luxon got started, but then he decided to talk about the Government’s track record, and the humour arrived unexpectedly! Three years ago, I said that if Christopher Luxon went into Government with David Seymour and Winston Peters, they would run circles around him. Well, it’s just as well they work in a round building, because they’ve run the carpet threadbare. I also said Christopher Luxon would have to get better at answering questions. On both of those predictions, I think I was right; on both of those predictions, we have seen no discernible improvement under this Government.
: They promised to fix the cost of living. They have made everything worse for New Zealanders. This is a Government that’s had the wrong priorities, that’s been out of touch with New Zealanders, and now, they are out of time as well. This is a Government that has been focused on their own jobs, not the jobs of New Zealanders.
: I want to share three stories in this adjournment debate speech which illustrate the real track record and the real New Zealand of this Government. The first is from Tauranga. An emergency department nurse came up to speak to me in a car park, and she said, “Mr Hipkins, I saw you on TV, and I wanted to say you were wrong, because you said that our emergency department was often in crisis, and you got that wrong. We are always in crisis under this Government.” Those nurses and doctors in our emergency departments feel like they are always in crisis. The numbers prove that and back them up. This Government has descended our health system into an absolute crisis, and they have no plan to fix it. Fifty-four new nurses in two years is the best they can do. Many of our hospitals have fewer nurses working in them today than they did three years ago. That is the track record of this Government. It is no wonder our hospitals are in absolute crisis. That emergency department nurse was right.
: The second person who I spoke to in the last few weeks was a business owner here in Wellington—
Rt Hon Christopher Luxon: Oh, yeah, that would be right—Wellington.
Rt Hon CHRIS HIPKINS: —a small business owner here in Wellington, a hospitality business owner here in Wellington. I know Christopher Luxon hates Wellington; he’s just proved that, once again, with his interjection. On Budget day, he said that from there on in, his turnover went down by $1,000 a day because this Government announced they were going to cut 9,000 more jobs. Those 9,000 job losses won’t just affect people working in the public sector; they will affect the private sector as well. That business lost $1,000 a day in turnover because of the axe that is now hanging over the jobs of 9,000 people. But it’s not just the 9,000 people; it’s everybody else who doesn’t know whether they’re going to be one of the 9,000 people who is now facing that uncertainty under this Government.
: The third story I wanted to tell was about people I spoke to in the supermarket at the weekend, a couple with a newborn baby, who came up—
Hon Member: In Wellington?
Rt Hon CHRIS HIPKINS: Yes, that was in Wellington. I live in Wellington. I live in Wellington. I speak to people here in Wellington. A couple came up to me while I was doing my supermarket shopping—which, coincidentally, Prime Minister, added up to a lot more than $60. They came up to me, and they said they just can’t make ends meet. They feel like they’re doing everything right. They go out to work—both of them work—and yet they can’t make ends meet. They’re doing everything that the country asks of them. They work hard, they contribute, and yet they don’t feel like they are better off with their own hard work. And they, like so many others, are considering leaving the country. Record numbers of New Zealanders have left the country under this Government, and the exodus is only going to continue if this Government gets re-elected. We cannot afford three more years of this Government.
: Let’s look at the track record that Christopher Luxon is supposedly so proud of: higher unemployment—50,000 New Zealanders who had jobs three years ago don’t have jobs now. That’s his Government’s shameful legacy. Youth unemployment is up, with nearly 100,000 New Zealanders under the age of 25 doing nothing. They’re not in education, they’re not in employment, and they’re not in training—nearly 100,000 New Zealanders. That is our future that this Government is writing off. Wages have been going backwards for New Zealanders, and this Government, the National Party and their mates, want to freeze wages for three more years. They’re not talking about freezing anybody’s costs. They’re not talking about freezing board directors’ fees, which they’ve hiked up by up to 80 percent. They’re saying that those people who go out and earn salaries and wages should have their wages frozen if they get re-elected. This country cannot afford three more years of this Government.
: Then there are the tens of thousands of women up and down the country that had their pay cut by this Government in the dead of night under urgency, because this Government doesn’t think the work of women is worth the same as the work of other New Zealanders. It was one of the most disgraceful and shameful things that I have seen happen in this Parliament, passing under urgency a law that took away pay equity from the woman who have worked so hard to get it—care and support workers who work hard in our rest homes, caring for our elderly in their own homes, now earning barely minimum wage under this Government. It says everything about where this Government’s priorities are. Eighty to 90 percent increases in fees for company directors, but pay equity for hard-working women in New Zealand gets cut.
: New Zealanders face a clear choice at this election. Where this Government promises more chaos, which is what we’ve had, we will offer the stability that New Zealand deserves. Where they promise more cuts, we will invest in New Zealand’s future. Where they offer fear, we will offer New Zealanders hope. Where they embrace conspiracy theories, we will back science. Where they offer arrogance and entitlement, we will offer humility and service, because that is what public service and politics should be about. While they offer blame, excuses, and word salad, we will offer honesty and answers—something this Government has spent three years avoiding delivering.
: Homelessness is up, and their excuse—their answer—to homelessness: just pass move-on orders; make the problem go away by making it less visible. KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals are at record levels, food prices are up, business liquidations are up, and attacks on migrants and Māori are happening more and more. This is disgraceful behaviour by this Government, and the National Party have a lot to say on a lot of issues but not when their own coalition partners attack migrant New Zealanders. They tout the India free-trade agreement, and yet they don’t mind Ministers in their own Government talking about a “butter chicken tsunami”. They had nothing to say in defence of migrant New Zealanders when that happened. They had nothing to say in defence of Chinese New Zealanders when the Minister of Foreign Affairs chose to attack them. They have nothing to say on the division that Ministers in this Government have been stoking. They’ve shown no leadership on those issues, and now they’re going to go cap in hand to those same communities and ask them to vote for them. Why should those communities vote for them when they weren’t willing to stand up for them in Parliament when their own Ministers were attacking them?
: Better is possible. Labour will offer New Zealanders real help with the cost of living, making sure that you can get to see a doctor and that you don’t have to go to a hospital emergency department because you can’t get in to see your doctor or you can’t afford to see a doctor; making sure public transport is more affordable for New Zealanders, with a public transport fare cap of $20 a week, or $10 a week in the provinces; making sure people can install solar panels on their roof; taking on the supermarkets; telling all New Zealand corporates that we will not tolerate price gouging in New Zealand—we will make sure Kiwis stop being ripped off and get a better deal—standing up for Kiwis in a way this Government has completely failed to do for three years; backing New Zealanders back into work by supporting the 97 percent of businesses in New Zealand that are small businesses, who have been completely forgotten by this Government; helping young New Zealanders into a trade by restoring the Apprenticeship Boost that was cut by this Government; taking action on AI, where our Government has been completely absent on one of the major issues facing humanity.
: This Government has completely failed to do the thing that it promised to do. They promised to fix the cost of living; they made it worse. They promised to get New Zealanders back to work; they’ve increased unemployment. They promised to fix the health system, and Kiwis are dying in hospital waiting rooms. This Government are out of ideas, and they are now out of time.
CHLÖE SWARBRICK (Co-Leader—Green): What I would say to you is that I want to start by thanking the workers who actually make this place tick. That is, the cleaners, the clerks, the security guards, the Chamber officers, the messengers, the librarians, the Coppers and catering staff, the team at the Parliamentary Service, and our dedicated lean Green parliamentary fighting team. Shout-outs to all of the press gallery, who are up there doing their best to report on the rolling trash fire that is this Government’s one term. Thank you, Mr Speaker, for finding a way to kick me out of Parliament more times this term than Winston Peters for the crime of asking whether we could find any Government MPs with a spine. For the record, I never actually said that the Government MPs were spineless; I simply asked if we could find six of 68 Government MPs with a spine to sanction Israel for its genocide in Gaza, but clearly we could not find an answer to that question. But, as we know, in this place you can’t say that something is racist if it is racist, and you cannot call a lie a lie. And, clearly, you can’t say that an MP is being spineless if that is what they are. It turns out you cannot even ask the question. You can, however, as this Government does every single day, serve its corporate mates.
: Let’s take a little moment to do a retrospective of what Christopher Luxon, Winston Peters, and that other guy have done with their three years in power. They came to office three years ago and reinstated the Resource Management Act, which the previous Government had already replaced. Then they spent three years complaining about that very Resource Management Act, which they had reinstated, only to finally claim victory yesterday by finally scrapping the law that they had put back in place. Congratulations, guys. It must have been really difficult to pat yourselves on the back for doing something that the last Government did, but worse.
: Then, before Christmas, under urgency in 2023, they revoked the Inland Revenue Department’s ability to report on the unfairness of our tax system. I wonder why the Taxpayers’ Union wasn’t up in arms about that one! But, then again, the Taxpayers’ Union was also missing in action when the Government chose to dish out $200 million in taxpayer money to subsidise new fossil fuels in the middle of a fossil fuel crisis. Of course, the problem, Christopher Luxon believes, is not with corporate greed; Christopher Luxon’s problem is not the bloated corporations that are ripping New Zealanders off on their energy and their grocery bills. His problem isn’t that our infrastructure is failing or that we are too dependent on imported fossil fuels and therefore exposed to imported inflation. No, Christopher Luxton’s problem is the environment, that pesky Treaty, those school kids and their lunches, the teachers, the nurses, the firefighters, the small businesses, and those pesky frogs.
: Nothing will get in the way of the Government’s growth agenda. Not the climate that is necessary for life on Earth as we know it. Not the health of our soil or our air or our water. Not those bloody fish in the oceans. Not the biodiversity on our public conservation land, and not the endangered geckos or skinks or moths. Indeed, Christopher Luxon has decided that it’s the kiwi who are the problem, getting in the way of all of those motorways that he thinks we need to build. It was a dedicated ministry for the environment that was the problem, so he disestablished that. Christopher Luxon decided that women actually are the problem, so he took away the rights of 300,000 of our lowest-paid working women to access pay equity. In fact, it’s actually renters who are the problem! So he passed law to allow landlords to evict 1.5 million people without any cause, undermining every single other right that they have.
: In Christopher Luxon’s New Zealand, it is the Public Service and the poor who are the problem, so his Government has cut benefits for the severely sick and disabled, pushed 47,000 more children into poverty, and intentionally increased homelessness to the highest levels that we have ever seen. But don’t worry, the Government has decided that they will just empower the police to move those homeless people out of sight and out of mind! Christopher Luxon has delivered us the highest unemployment that we have seen in 11 years. Then he decided that we’re going to sanction those who are struggling to find work. But don’t worry young people, Christopher Luxon has not forgotten about you! While one in three young New Zealanders is currently looking for more work that doesn’t exist in Christopher Luxton’s economy, he has decided to make those young people financially dependent on their parents, increase their tuition fees if they decide to turn to studying, and told them to just move to where the jobs are. So 178,000 New Zealanders have taken the Prime Minister’s advice, leaving their home and our country, along with taking their skills, their creativity, and their energy.
: But here comes the Government with the full power of the Public Service to tackle the real problems! Under their direction, this Parliament has spent hours and hours making English an official language, and the three men in charge of this country have decided to waste all of our time defining what a woman is. Here we are, in the middle of the campaign, and Captain Simeon Brown is at the helm. I was first introduced to his handiwork two decades ago almost, when we were both students at the University of Auckland. Lecture theatres had been littered with flyers filled with disinformation about abortions. Simeon’s Pro-life on Campus was later disaffiliated by Arena Williams from the Auckland University Students Association, but it was an early exposure to just how this man works. Now he’s graduated to big boy tax billboards and AI slop.
: Look, I know the National Party hates the arts and they hate artists, but you’d think with all of those corporate donations, perhaps they could pay some creatives to design their attack ads—although I will say one cool thing about all of these artificially generated illustrations of KiwiMart is just how popular it is. That’s the funny thing: this Government cannot run on its track record. It is, frankly, embarrassing. Instead, they have decided to attack the very idea that the Government could actually do something with the power that it is given to improve the lives of New Zealanders. In Christopher Luxon’s world, people don’t work together; they screw each other over to make as much money as possible. That is why this Government has no vision, no aspiration, no plan to bring us together to do the things that none of us could ever achieve alone. It wants us fighting each other as their donors laugh their way to the bank.
: The Greens believe in the power of New Zealanders. We believe in this plucky little country’s ability to lead the world. We believe that nature should flourish. We believe in fixing what is so obviously broken. We believe in making life easier, less exhausting, and, God forbid, more fun for all New Zealanders, and that is why we are in this building.
: I was actually probably a little bit dumb, given how long it took me to realise that that is not the same reason that all politicians are here. One day, early on in this term, when we were in the midst of one of the many urgency sessions spurred on by this Government’s lobbyist wish list, I must have had my head in my hands, and Rawiri Waititi turned to me and said something that made it all starts to make sense: “Politics is a game to these guys.” Politics can be a game when you’re wealthy and sorted. Politics can be a game when you’re entitled to your entitlements, Prime Minister. But politics is not a game when it is the difference between whether your family can eat, whether they have a roof over their head. Politics is not a game when you sit with the reality of the climate crisis. I know that means that we get a reputation for being uptight dorks. I know that it means that we get a reputation for being angry, but I make no apologies for caring about this country, because that is the point, if there has ever been one.
Hon Shane Jones: Drill, drill!
CHLÖE SWARBRICK: I want every New Zealander to know that, in the real world out there, Shane Jones, we here in this place are fighting for you, to fix the real basics necessary for all New Zealanders to live a decent life—for Te Tiriti o Waitangi, because it is indeed ironic that the Prime Minister doesn’t recognise Māori sovereignty despite his co-Deputy Prime Minister being the most self-sovereign individual that Parliament has ever seen. Winston Peters is living proof that Māori never ceded sovereignty.
: For affordable bills, healthy nature, and honest politics, the Greens are fighting for New Zealanders every single day, for a country that works for all of us.
Hon DAVID SEYMOUR (Deputy Prime Minister): Mr Speaker, thank you. I couldn’t help but think, if Chlöe Swarbrick’s speech just then needs background music, it could be set to “Help!” by The Beatles as a perfect accompaniment.
: I want to thank you, Mr Speaker, for this term of Parliament and your work; my coalition partners, fellow leaders Winston and Chris, for the way we’ve worked together more successfully than our worst enemies’ worst nightmares to put a record amount of legislation through this House, making New Zealand a better place. I particularly want to thank all of those who work across the parliamentary precinct, some 700 people, and especially my colleagues in the ACT Party, who have shown up every day with courage and conviction to make New Zealand a better and freer society. Particularly, I want to farewell Mark Cameron and Brooke van Velden. I think their valedictories, for us, have been highlights of the term—a pure expression of why they came here.
: I think, if we’re honest, this country faces some challenges that it has faced across Governments. Productivity growth has been too low, for 15 years at 0.2 percent. Houses have been too expensive, recently as high as 10 years’ income to buy one. These are challenges that require serious solutions, executed well, over time so that problems which grew up over a long period can be fixed.
: The most urgent need is, first of all, to lock Labour out of power, because we know that they won’t make it better, but worse. The Labour Party was soft on violent crime and gangs. You can’t trust them on law and order. If you can’t be safe on the streets, you can’t produce an honest buck. But, even if you can, you know they’ll tax it and then borrow $120 billion more, putting debt on to you and your grandchildren. When you hear these speeches, the visionless, energy-less nothing from cynical Chris Hipkins; the madness of business class Chlöe—and we can only dread what may be to come; hopefully at least a laugh from Rawiri—you see why it is so critical to lock Labour out.
: It is even more important—it is even more important—that we unlock this country’s potential. I would argue that the ACT Party has played a consistent, effective, and honourable role in this Government at unlocking this country’s potential. We do that in three ways. One is that we need a smaller, more efficient Government. We need to spend less and get better results. The ACT Party can point to $14 billion of savings from our Ministers and our policies over the last three years. We worked out that’s $57,000 for each person who voted for us. Now, when you consider it’s free to give your party vote to ACT, that’s got to be a good deal.
: We’ve also stopped three new taxes during this term of Government. We welcome new disciples to the “Church of No New Taxes”, no matter how recently they may have sinned. All are welcome. We know Chris has changed churches before, and we’re glad to see him at our one, preaching “no new taxes”. But there’s something more than that. We don’t just need to stop reaching for people’s money in new taxes; we must ensure that our Government is smaller and more efficient, has fewer Ministers, fewer departments, and has clear objectives, with one Minister in charge of one department, with one chief executive that they’re responsible for and can hire and fire. When you do that, you get a real focus on efficiency, which I don’t believe we’ve done enough of in this Government, but I’m proud of the effort that our party has made to ensure that the savings are there—a smaller, more efficient Government that delivers the medicines on time, that gets the children to school, that makes sure that they’re safe if they’re taken into custody by Oranga Tamariki, that the court system goes faster, and that you can even get your passport so fast it’s almost not worth paying for the rapid service.
: That’s just a few of the things that ACT Party Ministers have been up to in this Government. Even as Andrew Hoggard has acted as a one-man biosecurity defence army, keeping every kind of bug, from microbes to pests and—
Hon Andrew Hoggard: And hornets.
Hon DAVID SEYMOUR: He stopped the yellow-legged hornets by putting little devices on them. I mean, there is nothing that Andrew Hoggard cannot do in defence of the realm against biosecurity threats.
: The second thing we’ve got to do, other than have a smaller, more efficient Government, is be safe. We brought back three-strikes. We defunded cultural reports after we found the last Government was spending more on sob stories for convicted criminals before they were sentenced than they were spending on Victim Support. Then we said, “If you attack someone working sole charge or at a place that’s adjacent to their dwelling, that’s an extra crime.” But we’ve got to go further. We’re going to make it a crime to coerce someone by animal abuse, perhaps the most despicable crime in this country that I’ve been shocked to learn about in the last few years. We’re going to make sure we throw the book at it. We’re going to get tough on shoplifters, with accredited security guards, and we’re going to ensure that burglaries—if you get caught for three, you’ve probably done a heap, so you’re going to jail for three years for three-strikes burglary.
: Then there’s something else we’ve got to do to unlock the potential of this country and get prices down and productivity up, and that is stop the stupid rules and the red tape that has tied New Zealanders up in process instead of production. Again, this Government has made a fantastic start. We’ve done fast track. We’ve replaced the Resource Management Act with new laws based on property rights. We’ve got new medicines consented faster. We’ve got new agricultural and horticultural products consented faster. We’ve made sure that the Holidays Act has been replaced with something that actually makes sense for small business. The Ministry for Regulation has saved at least a quarter of a billion dollars by cutting red tape out, sector by sector by sector. This Government, I believe, will be seen as a turning point where we began to start saving money and saving time by stopping tying people up in red tape that draws people into process instead of production. That is work that we will continue in the next Government, carrying out a jihad on red tape so the potential of New Zealanders to produce more of the day, more creatively, with more Xeros and ZURUs, more Halters and Gallaghers. We’ll make sure that higher-paying jobs are available so New Zealanders can afford more of the things that we need.
: Finally, if we want to really unlock the potential of this country, we must ensure that we each are valued as human beings with hopes and dreams, with equal rights no matter when it was that our ancestors made the pioneering journey to these islands. We should not be judged differently based on which wave of migration brought our family here, whether it was in our own lifetimes—or, in my case, starting 600 years ago. We are all united as New Zealanders who made that journey, and I’m proud that, in this Government, when two patients come in for pre-diabetic medicine, they both get the same treatment, based on their clinical need now, not treated differently, where one pays and the other doesn’t because one’s ancestors came here at a different time. It’s the same with bowel cancer screening.
Hon Carmel Sepuloni: Oh David, that is not right.
Hon DAVID SEYMOUR: Yes, that is right. That’s exactly what we’ve done. Carmel Sepuloni needs to keep up. Then you look at the Māori Health Authority, gone; three waters, no longer co-governed. This Government has brought about one law for all and one future together. Yes, we started a debate no one else had the courage to start, let alone follow through, on the true meaning of our Treaty. It cannot be the case that our founding document is the Treaty, that the Treaty divides us into a partnership between races, and that we are a liberal democratic society. You can have any two of those, but not all three at the same time. That is why the ACT Party will continue to campaign for one law for all, one future together, equal rights before the law as human beings, not discriminated against on the basis of when our ancestors arrived in this country.
: This country has great potential; it has great hope. If we can ensure that the work of this coalition Government continues, that the streets remain safe because victims are the priority in the home, in the shop, and out in public; if we can ensure that the Government is smaller and more efficient—perhaps with 10 or 15 or 19 departments but far fewer than we have right now—and if we can ensure that we have a red tape jihad that frees people up to be more productive and spend less time in compliance activity; and if we can treat each other as New Zealanders, equal before the law, regardless of when we arrived, there is no limit to what we can achieve. There is no reason that we should not be the wealthiest country on Earth, and there is no reason we should not be proud to call New Zealand home, as the greatest society that humanity has ever known. Thank you, Mr Speaker.
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): As this Parliament adjourns, it’s appropriate to record our thanks to the cleaners, the library staff, the security teams, Hansard staff, committee clerks, chauffeurs, receptionists, and every other worker in this House, including yourself, Mr Speaker, your deputy, and assistant speakers.
: Now, adjournment debates are traditionally a time to outline a politician’s record in this House across the term of Parliament. Unlike others, we have the rare privilege of actually having a record. That is why we say thank you to Shane Jones, Casey Costello, Mark Patterson, Jenny Marcroft, and their teams supporting them in their Government portfolios and, indeed, to the entire New Zealand First caucus and our team.
: We are a party limited by the Standing Orders to only four member’s bills at any one time, but we have introduced 56 private member’s bills in the last term—56. That means we’ve done the work, we’ve done the research, we’re not all talk—fast on the lip and slow on the hip—no, we do the actual work.
: These bills represent—[Interruption]—no, you can cheer later; you can applaud later—new ideas in line with New Zealand First’s values of social conservatism, patriotism, economic nationalism, and common sense. Our bills will be ready to be adopted in the forthcoming coalition agreement, and members of our supporting governing parties will, no doubt, look forward to advancing the interests of the common man and woman in the next term of Parliament.
: We cannot get too far ahead of ourselves, because there is much too much good news to share in our record of this term. When New Zealand First makes an agreement, we keep our word. We’re famous for it too. You need to not judge us only by our words but by our deeds. We said the regions needed investment. We invested $1.2 billion into the regional infrastructure fund—money directed into productive and resilient assets around this country. Jobs, jobs, and jobs and wealth created in New Zealand with training chances for our young people.
: We said that the Therapeutic Products Act was the wrong law, overtly complicated, over-bureaucratic, and a threat to the natural health products sector. And it was repealed. We said young New Zealanders waiting for mental health assistance needed practical help right then with providers like Gumboot Friday. We kept our promise. By November last year, more than 40,000 counselling sessions had been delivered through the Gumboot Friday programme.
: We said English, the international language of commerce and the language used overwhelmingly in this House—including by the Greens, on a good day—should have the same statutory recognition of its official status that other official languages have. On 7 August this year, that became the law.
: We said New Zealanders were entitled to a wider examination of the country’s response to the COVID-19 occurrence and not a mark-your-own-homework exercise as happened under Labour. The expanded royal commission completed its work and delivered its final report in February this year. It found young people between 12 and 17 were given second doses when Chris Hipkins and Ayesha Verrall were told not to do that; 311,000 young people wrongly got the dose.
: Labour were found scurrying amongst nurses and teachers—meaning training professionals who were desperately, desperately needed in hospitals and classrooms—and they sacked them. They mandated them out of a job. And then they get in this House every day and talk about a lack of nurses and doctors—hundreds and hundreds of which they sacked. The Opposition yells about the need for more teachers and nurses—well, shame on them for mandating them out of the profession.
: We said our citizens deserved recognition and practical support. Budget 2026 funded the next generation of the SuperGold card, including the option of a free physical ID that seniors have long called for.
: Then there is the question of the infrastructure. While others campaigned to get our country back on track, you need look no further than New Zealand First to get evidence of who actually delivered it—$1.075 billion for rail network funding in Budget 2026. This is the first time ever a full three-year programme has been funded in advance—not fiscal cliffs like under Labour.
: On the Cook Strait: we fixed the ferries for road and rail, and we’re going to save $2.3 billion from the idiocy we inherited, where the ferries were going to cost 20 percent of the total cost. So you go to buy ferries and they spent 80 percent of the money on infrastructure. How foolish. Go look at Tasmania and see where that would have got us; $2.3 billion saved—
Hon Rachel Brooking: Government by text message—what a shameful way to govern!
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS: Don’t argue about the common sense of this. I know you’re slow. Can I ask you this question: what’s your business background? What’s your business background?
Hon Shane Jones: Zero!
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS: Zero—exactly. It ain’t hard to get it right when you have experience—unlike the last lot who pursued palatial department allowances and wanted to lift the arts so high that Noah could berth his ark. When the fuel crisis hit our shores, who ensured we finally sorted out increased storage at Marsden Point by nine days, just like that? That’s right, it was New Zealand First.
: Likewise, this House has finally grappled with the 1980s misadventure of the legal fraternity to invent Treaty principles. Now, I know imitation’s the most sincere form of flattery, but how many people now agree with us? Māori leaders like Ngata, Pōmare, Buck, and Carroll all understood the Treaty was a pact between two peoples to create one nation, one people under one flag and with one name. They understood the Treaty has no principles in it. This country has had it up to here with the wah-wah-wānanga delivering nothing but grievance founded on spurious words invented by the Labour Party. The country respects the Treaty signed in 1840—not the made-up nonsense written in those 1980s university clubhouses. That is why we have repealed those provisions with certain legislation—and we have more work ahead of us.
: That is what it looks like to understand reality. We know what a Treaty is; we know what a woman is—[Interruption]. Oh, it’s got them going. One more time: we know what a woman is—hush for a while—and we know what realpolitik looks like in foreign affairs. We’ve got the experience; the others are all talk.
: In our efforts, we have spent eight months abroad rebuilding New Zealand’s relationship with the world, including visiting all 17 Pacific member States and China—yes, I’ve been to China, not once but twice. Yes, I have a great relationship with China. Of course, I was the first guy to ever have a business connection with China when I did the export education in 1997—the first deal ever; you’ve all forgotten. So we’ve been offshore for eight months.
: But, look, we’ve spent more time in this House than every Māori Party MP combined, including the two who got chucked out. Now, tell me, what on earth is going on in the mainstream media when I have to tell you that information? All this time, since 1867, the law was changed to accept Māori into this Parliament and they don’t turn up, for the first time ever.
: Members, there is much more work ahead to fix this country. To govern a country, you need to know the ropes. The world is tough out there in reality and away from the cloistered comfort of the Green and Labour Party MPs in the leafy suburbs.
: We are the party who ensured the minimum wage, who lifted and strengthened the fast-track legislation to enable industry to create jobs for our own, and who knows what hard work looks like. New Zealanders are sick and tired of globalist ideologies capturing politicians and leading to industry closing down and people losing their jobs—
Hon Member: Tell us about the gays, Winston!
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS: Look, come to Tauranga on Saturday afternoon at 2 o’clock to Trinity—it’ll be wall to wall again. The only party that is filling the halls in this country—it’s called democracy, it’s called market share, and it’s called logic. Now come and learn; you just might find out something.
: You see, the Greens have been here trying for Parliament since 1972; 54 years and they’ve never been in Cabinet—54 years, never been in Cabinet.
Francisco Hernandez: And we’re still bigger than you, mate. You won’t be around next time. Bye-bye, Winston! Bye-bye, Winston!
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS: Oh, “Bye-bye, Winston!” Stand back, sunshine; I’ve got news for you. I’m coming back real big-time. We’re coming back with an army. We’re going to come back much bigger. Oh, don’t wave out to me. You should get up shortly and make your valedictory speech, because you guys are going to be out of here. No, we’re coming back—not for the first time. Out there, there are hundreds of thousands of people who’ve realised one thing: there’s a party that understands this country better than any other and that offers real hope for tomorrow. Thank you very much.
RAWIRI WAITITI (Co-Leader—Te Pāti Māori): Thank you. How generous. Thank you for that applause. Ngā mihi nui ki a koe e te Pīka. This is the second time I’ve mihi-ed you today. I just want, again, to pass on these sentiments and thank you for the hard mahi, and also to all the staff here in Parliament for making the House work. This is my last speech I will give in the House under this Government, but like Arnold Schwarzenegger said, I’ll be back. This has been the most anti-Māori, anti-Tiriti, anti-taiao, anti-worker Government in a generation, and they have finally run out of numbers on the clock. On 7 November, we will issue their move-on orders from this House.
: This is a Government that challenged our resilience, who we are forced to activate against, and although we couldn’t count on them, we have run their numbers. It took them two days to disestablish Te Aka Whai Ora. They removed 24 Māori wards from local councils across Aotearoa; that’s 24 tables that will no longer have an unapologetic Māori voice. A hundred thousand voters—that’s how many people will be disenfranchised because the Government’s parties are afraid of our voting power. A hundred and eighty thousand women—that’s how many hard-working wāhine had their pay equity claims cancelled under urgency so that this Government could give out handouts to landlords and corporations.
: They removed section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act, and they have weakened Treaty obligations across education, pae ora, and the Resource Management Act. There are 19 more Treaty clauses that they will weaken or remove if we don’t vote this Government out. Four million dollars—that’s how much taxpayer money was wasted on the failed Treaty principles bill. Fifty days—that’s how long Te Pāti Māori MPs were suspended from this House for daring to challenge the most racist and ignorant bill of this century. This Government overturned at least three major court decisions; they entrenched the theft of our foreshore and seabed with the marine and coastal area amendment bill; they protected the biggest polluters in Aotearoa from litigation; and they legalised the killing of those, Chlöe, pesky kiwis. They have prioritised the erasure of our rights and privilege of our whenua—wow.
: Over 112,000 people in Aotearoa don’t know where they’re sleeping tonight. One in seven tamariki is living in poverty. One in four tamariki Māori is living in poverty. Māori continue to die seven years earlier than non-Māori, and Māori unemployment has gone from 6.8 percent to 10.8 percent under this Government’s watch. These are the numbers under this Government, yet when Te Pāti Māori challenges the lived reality of te iwi Māori in this House, we are met by excuses and justifications centred in statistics of crime reduction and incarceration. A Government that measures the success of te iwi Māori in crime reduction is one content with keeping our people incarcerated. A Government that measures its wealth in the tax breaks afforded to the 2 percent is one content with keeping its country in a cost of living crisis. A Government that measures its “clean, green” New Zealand image in only tourism sales is one content on allowing mining and drilling and the further degradation of whenua Māori for profit. A Government that measures its unity in the regression of equitable policies is one that doesn’t understand Te Tiriti o Waitangi and has never read Matike Mai.
: When Te Pāti Māori stands in this House, this Government calls statements performative. I would argue that should be said for the Government’s ability to create positive change for this country. The Prime Minister can reject the characterisation of our questions in the House, but we reject how this House characterises te iwi Māori. Despite everything this Government has subjected te iwi Māori to over this term, and the harmful rhetoric and narratives they have generated, I want to share the real stories, and stats, our people live in: 312,000 people are on the Māori roll; 100,000 people hikoi-ed  against the Treaty principles bill and this Government; 300,000 submitted against the Treaty principles bill; and te iwi Māori’s population is now almost one million.
Hon Member: 30 seconds.
RAWIRI WAITITI: Our stats live—point of order. I was under the understanding we all get 10 minutes?
SPEAKER: No, it’s a split call.
RAWIRI WAITITI: It’s a split call.
SPEAKER: Yeah, sorry.
RAWIRI WAITITI: I will go to the back page, Mr Speaker; 8 November will be an opportunity for New Zealand to see a brand new Government. If you want to see more Māori in Parliament, if you want to see a one-term Government, and to maintain an unapologetic Māori voice, the only way you can do that is candidate vote Te Pāti Māori. That is how we do that. This is the last stand that this Government will make. Come 7 November, you’ll be bye, bye, goodbye. Kia ora tatou.
Hon MARAMA DAVIDSON (Co-Leader—Green): Democracy should work for all of us, not just the wealthy few. Te Tiriti has always been about taking the best possible care of each other, but right now a handful of very rich and powerful corporations can buy access and influence the Government for their private benefit.
: In 2024, an Ipsos survey revealed that two-thirds of people feel that the economic system is rigged totally in favour of the rich and the powerful. Yet, it is Te Tiriti that has been weaponised as being divisive, despite the generosity that Māori have shown to all people for generations, whether it is marae opening up when the roads are closed, feeding and caring for multitudes of strangers with the utmost manaaki, whether it is iwi and hapū restoring the health of our rivers and oceans, native forests, and native taonga species for all of our mokopuna to enjoy, whether it is iwi and hapū providing social and health services to whoever needs it in their communities.
: They label Te Tiriti as being divisive, despite the overwhelming majority of select committee submissions from the public and diverse organisations pleading to the Government that Te Tiriti and the relationships with local Māori have been vital to improving their work; that’s churches, unions, local and regional governments, local businesses, even developers, environmental groups, migrant groups, professional bodies, health bodies, and just ordinary members of the public who outright reject the attempts of these Government parties to sow division, who come with all the receipts of how Te Tiriti is one of the last bastions of protection for the environment, for workers, and for a community voice. That is why Te Tiriti is the target: because it stands in the way of the outright exploitation of our living systems, of workers’ rights and safety, and of community voice.
: Which brings us back to where the real, unelected representation has always been, and it’s not Māori on boards wanting to ensure there is accountability for environmental protection that benefits everybody. No, the real unelected representation has always been the underhand, backdoor connections between political parties who are refusing to tax their billionaire and big corporate donors, and who instead want working people like tradies and nurses and the local barbers to keep paying twice the effective tax rate of someone who owns 50 houses. To copy and paste the demands of the wealthy straight into their law; that is where the real divide has always been.
: The good news is that the Green Party will take big money out of politics. We will cap political donations at $30,000 and ensure that only people can donate and not companies. The Green Party has consistently stood by our values and our evidence-based policy solutions, to prioritise the wellbeing for the many and not just the few. We have not just a powerful opportunity to get rid of this Government, who have shown outright that they are here to serve billionaires, and bugger everyone else, but people have the chance to demand a Government that prioritises affordable living, healthy nature, and democracy for all of us, not just the powerful. Thank you.
Hon NICOLA WILLIS (Minister of Finance): Well, I thought that was a very good example of the co-leadership in action. Marama Davidson has certainly been taking Chlöe Swarbrick’s advice to touch grass. I think the only problem is there is such thing as touching too much grass.
: Colleagues, this is a time for gratitude, and I want to express some gratitude to a few people; first of all, to you, Mr Speaker: this is the first term of Parliament I have not been kicked out once, and I want to recognise you for that. Thank you.
SPEAKER: Well, thank you for highlighting my failures.
Hon NICOLA WILLIS: Ha, ha! In particular, I want to acknowledge the extremely special piece of correspondence I received from you—in your handwriting—reminding me, as the Minister of Finance, of the existence of the Parliament Act 2025. I shall always treasure that correspondence.
: I want to also acknowledge the staff at Copperfields, especially the baristas who pour long blacks directly into my veins, along with all of the unsung heroes of the precinct: the cleaners, the messengers, security guards, the Crown car drivers. These people don’t just deliver apricot danishes—but they do do that—they provide numerous moments of genuine kindness every day in this place. Chamber staff, Office of the Clerk, Parliamentary Counsel Office, Parliamentary Library, researchers—all these people who keep the democracy going. The members of the Press Gallery: in an age of declining trust, short-format video, clickbait, you soldier on and democracy is better for it, thank you.
: I want to acknowledge my caucus colleagues in the National Party, and also our dedicated National Party members and volunteers all over the country. They are the very, very best people, and I am so looking forward to campaigning with them.
: Our coalition colleagues: it has been an honour to have delivered this country’s first three-way coalition, and boy oh boy, have we got stuff done. Yes, there have been things on which we have differed, but we have gotten so much done for the good of this country.
: I want to acknowledge the agency staff, especially, in my case, the Budget and fuel response teams; departmental private secretaries; my extraordinary political office staff, who have saved me from so many potential troubles, and whose grace and kindness continues to astound me.
: But I feel that while we have achieved a lot for New Zealand—the first tax relief in 14 years; Investment Boost, ensuring tax incentives for those investing in growth and development; extending contributions to KiwiSaver; the tightest spending allowances in years, and yet prioritising investments in things that really matter: 33 new cancer drugs on our watch; the biggest boost for special education in our schools in decades; the FamilyBoost payment to help parents with the costs of early childhood education; funds in each of our Budgets to restore the dignity of the New Zealand Defence Force and the men and women who put their lives on the line for our country; backing our police; building infrastructure; getting things done.
: But it is wrong in a speech like this to save all congratulations for the Government. I do want to recognise the Opposition. I really want to hand out some awards to them. I think the first thing we need to recognise is that if Parliament handed out medals for political gymnastics, Labour would have swept the podium this term. Yesterday, in a routine that would have scored a perfect 10 from the East German judge, Chris Hipkins performed the finest backflip this House has seen in a very long time. For three years, that member, backed up by his chorus of MPs, has practised one routine and one routine only. For every problem that has been ever described under this fair sun, he has had something to blame: it’s the tax cut for landlords! Interest deductibility—that was the problem. Whether it was the cost of living, whether it was unemployment, whatever it was, the problem was tax cuts for landlords. But then yesterday, we had a dismount, and we had—what I’ve been told they call in gymnastics—is a case of the “twisties”. Now, what happens with the twisties is that when you’re rotating in mid-air, you suddenly lose your sense of direction—completely lose your sense of direction—don’t know what’s up, what’s down, where you’re going, what you’re doing, and you panic. You panic in mid-air when you get the twisties, and I think this is what happened to Chris Hipkins yesterday. He was in mid-air, he realised he had no plan, he had no policies, he had no energy for the campaign, and he went, “Actually, I’m going to flip it and reverse it. That is exactly what he did.
: Speaking of routines gone wrong: Ginny Andersen—can we just recognise her? She tried her signature move on live radio a few weeks ago, telling Mark Mitchell that road maintenance is not funded by the National Land Transport Fund. “You don’t even know what you’re talking about.”, she told him. “It’s a separate fund—you need to go check that.”—you need to go check that—“[if] you want to be credible on financial things, then you’re really kidding yourself.” She learned the truth during the ad break: there is no separate fund for road maintenance. She attempted a Hipkins-like backflip to correct herself, face planted on the mat, and then— this is the impressive part—got up and instead insisted that the beam had moved.
: She is said to be receiving some coaching from Willie Jackson, her senior colleague, who is a master at never letting the facts, or your absence of policy, get in the way of the story. In fact, in Willie’s experience, the best way not to let the policy get in the way is to be blissfully unaware of it—that way, you don’t even have to defend it, you can just say, “I don’t know, ask Barb.”
: This is actually someone I do want to spend some time on. On the one hand, I see in the member for Mana, a lack of imagination—51 times she’s asked me the same question this term. But on the other hand, I feel genuine sympathy for Barbara Edmonds, and let me let me tell you why: because she is surrounded by people who know one thing and one thing only, and that is how to spend other people’s money. That’s what they’ve done all their political careers, and that’s what they want to do with the rest of their political careers. They have gone out there and they’ve promised, so far, $18 billion worth of promises. And they’ve said, “Barb will tell you how she’s going to pay for it”. Barbara’s been sitting there with the calculator, trying to make it add up, and she knows it won’t add up. Maybe one of the little fig leaves she was holding on to with hope was, “Well, I think the leader will let me raid the landlords for the interest deductibility. I think I’ll do that.”—but, no, even that little glimmer of hope was taken away from her yesterday. But the good thing for Barbara is she knows that in a case of emergency, she can break glass. What is in that little glass that she can break if she really can’t make it add up? Well, the good news is Craig Renney’s got some ideas.
: He’s been a bit painful for her, he’s been kind of competing for the role, but Chris Hipkins put him down the list, so he’s got his message. But he has come up with the idea—he said, “Look, this whole idea on a capital gains tax (CGT), don’t make it narrow, make it comprehensive.”, and that’s his plan. I just want to say with friends likeCarmel Sepuloni, Barbara—I don’t know how you do it. She was asked, on Morning Report, how Labour was going pay for its promises, and this is what she opened with: “Well, we certainly wouldn’t be giving tax breaks to landlords.” That was her answer! Poor Barbara, she’s left there going, “How on Earth do I make it up?”
: But here’s the thing—actually look at the mates they’ve got in the Greens and Te Pāti Māori. Yes, Chris Hipkins is half baked and he’s got no energy and he’s got no policies, but look, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori are brimming with ideas, they’re generating new taxes every minute. And don’t worry: Chris Hipkins says. “Well, trust us, we’ve sort of ruled it out.” This is the same guy who said he’d never deliver a CGT—and what’s he campaigning on? A CGT. If the leader of the Opposition can backflip on tax deductibility in the space of one press conference, why should anyone believe a thing he rules out between now and polling day? You can’t trust Labour on tax. You can’t trust Hipkins. There is a way forward for this country, we stick to the plan—no new taxes. Don’t let Labour ruin it all again.
SPEAKER: The Hon—[Interruption] At least start with a bit of silence. I call The Hon Carmel Sepuloni.
Hon CARMEL SEPULONI (Deputy Leader—Labour): In about 6½ weeks, the Hon Nicola Willis is going to look back on that speech and think, “Is that really the valedictory I wanted to deliver?”
: I do want to reiterate some of the thanks to the staff that have been given by many of those that have spoken before me today. I also want to acknowledge you, Mr Speaker, even though Willie Jackson is speaking to you—not the first time that Willie Jackson has interrupted anyone—and, Mr Speaker, I want to acknowledge that I sit rather close to you and I do have a voice that carries—
SPEAKER: Yep.
Hon CARMEL SEPULONI: —so thank you for your tolerance over the course of this term.
: I’m going to take a slightly different tack and acknowledge the fact that we are all going into campaign mode. Campaigns are hard work. They are not for the faint-hearted. I’m pretty seasoned now—not as seasoned as some in here—and as an experienced campaigner, I thought I’d offer up some do’s and don’ts to Government parties as we all head out into the wilderness of the campaign trail. These particular words of advice that I’m going to offer up are based mostly on the learnings of the past three years, observing the members of current Government parties, a Government that will go down in history as the coalition of chaos, and a Government that will be the first ever one-term National Government.
: Now, what not to do on the campaign trail. My first piece of advice: do not ride scooters on the campaign trail. As we all know, our emergency departments do not have the capacity, let alone the nurses, to deal with avoidable injuries, particularly given there’s been only 54 additional nurses added over the last two years.
: Second piece of advice: steer away from discussing sports teams when you know nothing about sport.
