No one wants to be the guy who refers to his childhood respect for the Crusaders when the Crusaders did not even exist during his childhood; and no one wants to be the guy that gets the Waratahs and the Warriors confused.
: Do not say, “What I would say to you”. People can see and hear when someone is talking out loud. You are not thinking in your head. There is no need to premise every answer with that statement. Best not to talk about growth, growth, growth, Nicola Willis. When people hear National say those words three times in a row, they think they are referring to the growth in unemployment, the growth in business liquidations, and the growth in Kiwis moving overseas. Even if the three words were said by Nicola Willis whilst she was clicking her heels together, no one would end up in a better place.
: Please, also—and this is a serious one—do not pretend to be political parties who support women. Women are not stupid. The scrapping of pay equity and the decision not to pay women what they are worth will go down in the books as one of the most shameful acts of this Luxon-led Government.
: Now, on to the do’s for the campaign. It’s important for politicians to sound like they are in touch with the everyday experiences of New Zealanders. Telling them to cry you a river when talking about the cost of living is out of touch. Try hard, Government parties, to be honest about the alternative policy positions of other parties. People will tire of lies about taxes. I know how hard it must be for the current Government having nothing positive to talk about after three years, but people can sniff the desperation, and it is not mana-enhancing for any of you.
: What parties must do is look like they actually support their boss. Two failed coups in National haven’t helped with their boss’s credibility. To be honest, you already look like the try-hard dad in the schoolyard or at the PTA meeting before his own team turned on him. I know that’s a little bit mean, but so was scrapping pay equity.
: Most importantly, keep at the forefront of all statements and actions what is important to New Zealanders. Their jobs; not the jobs of politicians. Their health; not the healthy size of some political party donations. Their homes; not the multiple homes of those politicians trying to avoid a capital gains tax. Their cost of living; not the $60 a week one guy reckons is all he needs to do his grocery shopping. And finally, their country; the one thing they love, and the one thing they feel has gone backwards. It may hurt Government parties whilst out on the campaign trail when they hear people say over and over again that they simply cannot do three more years of this National-led Government. Suck it up and remember: “Better starts now”.
Hon WILLIE JACKSON (Labour): Well, that’s the end of the most anti-Māori, anti-worker, anti-rainbow, anti-disability, anti - New Zealand Government that we have seen in our lifetime. You’ve got to ask yourself, why are they so weak? Well, because they’ve got a weak Prime Minister, who has allowed David Seymour and Winston Peters to take this country to a place that would shame Chris Finlayson, shame Jim Bolger, and shame Sir Douglas Graham.
: The Prime Minister can’t control New Zealand First and ACT, and they have polled 6 percent and 8 percent. My God, imagine the nightmare—imagine the nightmare and the influence—if they return with greater majorities. We’ll fight to make sure this never happens.
Hon Shane Jones: Bye, bye, Willie. Haere rā, haere rā!
Hon WILLIE JACKSON: We’ll never forget what they’ve done—never forget what they’ve done. Their assault on Te Tiriti obligations. The Waitangi Tribunal found the Crown’s approach to the education changes breaches Treaty principles. That means nothing to Shane Jones. He’s a disgrace to his people in the North. He no longer supports principles he formerly supported when he was a young, recognised, and principled young man.
: This racist friction that came about through the Treaty principles referendum cannot be complete without us acknowledging the honourable member for Epsom; the member who, this year, has managed the extraordinary feat of introducing a bill, losing it in the largest protest march in New Zealand history, and then telling us all he won. I mean, how delusional is that? The Treaty principles bill, 300,000 submissions against; the Regulatory Standards Bill opposed by every major Māori organisation, every legal academic who submitted, and at last count, the entire common-sense caucus of New Zealand; but the member for Epsom marches on, because he’s on a mission—a mission to erase kaupapa Māori and change the Treaty.
: Meanwhile, on the National benches, the Prime Minister, whose biggest achievement this term was to fend off Chris Bishop and Erica Stanford and his mates—we want to thank the Prime Minister. We want to thank him very much for staying the Prime Minister. He’s Labour’s best chance of winning this election. He’s not here, but I wanted to thank him and acknowledge his acknowledgment of me earlier in the day.
Hon Mark Mitchell: And you’re our best chance of staying in Government.
Hon WILLIE JACKSON: You know this, Mark Mitchell; you’re in big trouble. When you look at the Public Service and what’s happened here, at a time when every second news story is about the Public Service failing in terms of underfunding, they attack the Public Service. Look at the economic vandalism that sees one in three Pacific kids in poverty, one in four Māori kids in poverty, 5.6 percent unemployment, 10.8 percent unemployment for Māori. And, of course, let’s not forget the fast-track development that weakened environmental protections—
Hon Shane Jones: Fast track! Gold! Gold!
Hon WILLIE JACKSON: —for Shane Jones’ donor mates. For Shane Jones—that’s what the Greens said—and for their mates. We’ll never forget the school lunches, where hungry kids became an experiment in how cheaply lunch could be made, thanks to Mr Seymour again. What about the appalling pay parity betrayal? New Zealand women must never forget the betrayal of this coalition Government. New Zealand women do not count for this Government. They are a disgrace. Pay parity means so much to us, and we will change the position and reinstate equity.
: This Government came to office promising to fix the basics. Instead, they have made it worse. Three years later, unemployment rose, thousands of public servants went, hungry kids became the norm, environmental protections were weakened, and Māori spent the term watching rights and Treaty obligations stripped from statute after statute.
: They told New Zealand they were cutting bureaucracy, then spent three years restructuring the machinery of government. Hon LOUISE UPSTON (Leader of the House): Thank you, Mr Speaker. I think, for anyone who is watching, they can tell it is the last day of school. It is the last day of the 54th Parliament. As the member of Parliament for Taupō—the very proud member of Parliament for Taupō—I do want to just reflect on this period of time. Every single one of the 123 members of Parliament who have sat in this House serve a number of people in their communities, and they do it with the best intent. But, today, primarily I rise as the Leader of the House, and I want to acknowledge our Prime Minister, the Rt Hon Christopher Luxon, and the privilege that he gave me in serving in this role. I want to acknowledge the support of my predecessor, the Hon Chris Bishop. We’ve worked together very closely over this term.
: Most people look at this House, they look at this Chamber, as an amphitheatre of war, where members go into battle each and every day, and it’s something to win, something to endure—blood, sweat, and tears lie on the floor. It’s all about the legislative outcomes that people are willing to fight for, and that’s the end result, the political fight, the war which captures the media headlines. What is often not reported is the amount of work that goes in to getting a bill before this Parliament. I want to just run through some of the stats of the 54th Parliament, the collective efforts of the National Party, New Zealand First, and ACT: 230 pieces of legislation—210 Government bills, 14 members’ bills, four private bills, two local bills; 240 bills have been introduced by our Government this term. Yes, sometimes it’s felt like a bit of a political marathon. My thanks to this side of the House, who have endured many hours of urgency, overtime, over time. I do have to say the Hon Paul Goldsmith takes the gold medal for the most legislation, with 34 bills enacted. Chris Bishop comes up second, with 23. I’m a little bit down the medal table, on only 10. I do want to acknowledge the amount of effort that goes into each and every one of those bills—hundreds and hundreds of hours to get those pieces of legislation ready.
: I want to acknowledge some of the unsung heroes in the parliamentary process. Firstly, we are blessed in this country with phenomenal public servants. They work incredibly hard to deliver for the Government of the day policy solutions to the problems that our communities and our countries face. Then there is the Parliamentary Counsel Office, more commonly known as PCO. They do incredibly hard yards, translating the policy ideas into legislation, and they often, in our term of Parliament, have had tight time frames to do that. I do want to acknowledge and shout out Cassie Nicholson KC, who is the Chief Parliamentary Counsel, and Richard Wallace, the Deputy Chief Parliamentary Counsel, who have been incredibly helpful for our Parliament and our Government, working through an enormous amount of legislation. There’s also the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet. There is also the legislation coordinator in the Cabinet Office and all of the staff who support the legislative process for our Cabinet committees. Of course, then, when it comes here, it is the Clerk’s team who are really significant in terms of making sure everything is correct according to the Standing Orders. There are also other teams that make sure the Parliament runs as best as it can. As well as the Clerk’s Office, there is the select committee staff, and Hansard.
: I also want to draw on my own experiences of the 54th Parliament and reflect on the people in my own team who have helped progress those 10 pieces of legislation. In our team, we call it the “middle office”. Thank you to you all. I also want to thank somebody whose name is probably on more emails that run around this Parliament than anybody else. Of course, he would never have put his own name in a speech, but I do want to acknowledge my trusted House adviser Carlos Webster, who makes sure, with lots of challenges at times, that the legislation gets through the House on time. Also, as in every Minister’s office—and in our office, we call it the “Team Upston Class of 54”—there is an enormous team of private secretaries who are seconded from agencies. Every Minister has them. They are absolutely worth their weight in gold. I think the private secretaries who work in the Beehive are a particular special breed of public servants who deserve our acknowledgment today.
: As I approach the end of my speech, I also want, given it’s the end of the 54th Parliament, to offer a shout-out to the Opposition members. We do know that, in terms of accountability, question time is a really important part of this process. The public must have confidence that Ministers will be questioned robustly and—Mr Speaker and your presiding officers—if they transgress, they will be held to account. I’m reliably informed that, during the 54th Parliament, I have faced 153 primary questions, with only 99 of them coming from the other side. It is a really important part of the process.

National has continued to restore law and order, making New Zealand safer and putting victims at the heart of our justice system. We have been getting our kids back to school, teaching the basics and setting them up for life. And, of course, now, what are we doing? We are building the future. We are growing the economy to create more jobs and better opportunities for New Zealanders. We are maintaining disciplined spending so taxes are spent wisely. We’re upgrading roads, schools, hospitals, and giving Kiwis quality and reliable public services. By securing affordable housing for families and first-home buyers, hard-working Kiwis will have the security of owning their own home.
: Do you know what, Mr Speaker? I thank you, and I thank your presiding officers, but I want to particularly thank the National Party team. You’re an extraordinary group of New Zealanders. I know how hard you work. I know how dedicated you are to serving our communities and our country, and I feel enormously proud to be part of team National. And guess what! We’ll be back after 8 November. We’ll be here to do it all over again for the 55th Parliament. There are two things to remember: firstly, under National, there will be no new taxes; and if that’s what you want, you’ve got one choice before the 7 November, and that is party vote National.
SPEAKER: It’s usual, at the conclusion of this debate, for the Speaker to offer not only some thanks but also some statistics to the House, but Louise, you’ve just completely stolen my thunder, which leaves me—
Hon Member: Kick her out!
SPEAKER: I’m sure she’d be pleased to go, but it leaves me with some stats that aren’t quite so exciting, like Copperfields having sold 166,000 cups of coffee; 18,000 scones—Bish, where’s he; 5,690 doughnuts—that’s you, Willie, I think, is it? Oh no, it’s the pies, Willie—12,000 pies. Are you putting your hand up, Duncan?
Hon Dr Duncan Webb: Could be me.
SPEAKER: Yeah, it could be. Most of all, I was asked if I would say that the brilliant catering manager, Mr Bryce Hughes, has a personal favourite, which is the 1,000 servings of mince on toast.
: I want to put on the record an acknowledgment of all the work that all the members of this House have done over the past three years. It’s not an easy job and, as many have mentioned in their speeches, it does affect families and it does take people away from all of the normal things that people might do in life, and you do that because you have that commitment to the democratic process.
: Inside of that, there’s always this talk about the hours that we work here. There’s a lot of people today mentioning urgency, etc. Breaking it down, this House does about 600 hours—or, over the last three years, about 615 hours a year. It may not seem a lot if people hear that in a bald sort of way, but the time that MPs put into all of the knowledge that they bring into this House, all of the views they bring to this House, and all of the ideas they bring to this House is extraordinary, and I don’t think we should allow people to get too fixated on the time that people spend here in the House. There are always people away doing stuff. What I’ve learnt as Speaker, working with the whips, who I really do have a lot of respect for, is that there is an enormous number of things that people do that require them to be away from this House, and I fully respect that.
: I just want to add my thanks to the Clerk’s Office for the work that they do, not only with select committees but also here in the Chamber, and the Chamber staff as well. I want to thank the Chief Executive’s Office for the work they do in making everything that is Parliamentary Service work for members, and I want to thank the security staff for the work that they are doing. Security is one thing that we’ve had to improve significantly over the last three years, and the staff here have picked up on that extremely well, with a great deal of pride, and they now also work, of course, outside of Parliament should any of us need them.
: I want to mention the catering staff. They do a great job. I mentioned them before. I also want to—
Hon Members: Ha, ha!
SPEAKER: Well, look, imagine what it’d be like spending your time making 5,000 doughnuts. You’ve got to respect that. I also want to thank my executive assistant Laree Taula, and I also want to thank Kellie for stepping in when Roland Todd retired. I also want to thank Alyson Groves, from Parliamentary Service, who has done 42 years here and is about to retire, as well. I should thank the triumvirate of advice that I’ve had over the last three years, and part of that triumvirate is Dr David Wilson, who’s our Clerk and is a very learned man, and I’ve enjoyed our discussions with him; and also Rafael Gonzalez-Montero, the Chief Executive of Parliamentary Service, who genuinely has the best interests of members at heart; and also, the person that makes them both good, Andie Lindsay, in the joint office, who I’m sure everyone knows.
: I want to thank the VIP drivers—I’m just going through my list here—and I also need to thank Barbara Kuriger, Greg O’Connor, Teanau Tuiono, and Maureen Pugh for the work that they have done, sitting in here for those long hours of committee.
: With those remarks, can I wish everyone well as we go out on to the campaign trail, allowing New Zealanders to make a choice about how they want to be governed, in one of the freest democracies in the world.
: Motion agreed to.
: The House adjourned at 5.55 p.m.

conclusion: With those remarks, can I wish everyone well as we go out on to the campaign trail, allowing New Zealanders to make a choice about how they want to be governed, in one of the freest democracies in the world.

content.text: Wednesday, 23 September 2026
The Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.
Start of Sitting Day

content.speaker: TEANAU TUIONO (Assistant Speaker)

Ka mihi mātou ki te Kīngi, me te inoi atu mō te ārahitanga i roto i ō mātou whakaaroarohanga, kia mōhio ai, kia whakaiti ai tā mātou whakahaere i ngā take o te Whare nei, mō te oranga, te maungārongo, me te aroha o Aotearoa. [Almighty God, we give thanks for the blessings which have been bestowed on us. Laying aside all personal interests, we acknowledge the King and pray for guidance in our deliberations that we may conduct the affairs of this House with wisdom and humility, for the welfare, peace, and compassion of New Zealand. Amen.]
Speaker's Statements
Steve Streefkerk—Serjeant-at-Arms

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Members, I’d like to notify the House that today marks the last sitting day that Steve Streefkerk, the Serjeant-at-Arms, will bear the mace. Steve has served in this role since 2016, after a distinguished naval career, including being Commander of HMNZS Te Kaha. We thank him for his dedicated service and wish him well for his next role.
Privilege
Development of Framework for Recommendations for Punishing Members for Contempt
Referral to Privileges Committee

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Members, the Standing Orders Committee has presented its report on the Review of Standing Orders 2026. The report will be debated today. One of the committee’s recommendations is that a general question of privilege be referred regarding a framework for reaching recommendations for punishing members for contempt.

Historically, it has been very rare for the Privileges Committee to recommend that a member be suspended from the service of the House. There are only two known examples prior to this term of Parliament: one was for one day and one was for three days. The suspension of members in this term for as long as three weeks therefore represents a change in the House’s practice.

In its report, the Standing Orders Committee said it would be useful for a framework to be developed for how punishments for contempt may be determined in the future. Such a framework or set of expectations would support the Privileges Committee in reaching recommendations that are seen as proportionate and consistent.

A framework could set out factors for the Privileges Committee to consider when recommending punishments. It could also indicate steps to ensure a robust and fair process. For the public to have confidence in the House’s disciplinary procedures, it is important to avoid perceptions that they may be arbitrary in their operation.

Although I can refer a question of privilege without a recommendation to do so, I believe the Standing Orders Committee’s report provides useful context for why a referral should be made. Accordingly, I find that a general question of privilege arises and stands referred to the Privileges Committee. I expect that consideration to be undertaken and commenced when the committee reconvenes in the next Parliament.

Points of Order
Ministers—Correction of Statements

content.speaker: RICARDO MENÉNDEZ MARCH (Musterer—Green)
content.text: Point of order. Thank you very much, Mr Speaker. I just want to raise a serious matter on Ministers taking the first available opportunity to correct inaccurate or potentially misleading statements. This is the last opportunity a Minister has to do so. On the 15th of this month, Minister Louise Upston, when asked whether she had sought advice on the impact on sick, injured, and disabled New Zealanders and whether they had been left into debt, homelessness, or hunger, answered yes. I posed the very same question in writing, and, today, just now, a couple of hours ago, she came back to me with the exact opposite answer, which was an emphatic no. I’m concerned that Ministers are not taking the opportunity to correct statements when a week ago I got an emphatic yes to a question and in writing got a very clear no to the very same question.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Yeah, look, it’s fairly straightforward. I think the procedure for such contested responses like that is to either write to the Speaker or set down a notice of motion on the Order Paper. I appreciate that we are at the end of this Parliament, but, none the less, the Standing Orders remain in place.
Oral Questions to Ministers
Finance
Question No. 1

content.speaker: RYAN HAMILTON (National—Hamilton East)
content.text: to the Minister of Finance: What has been the Government’s approach to tax in this parliamentary term?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLA WILLIS (Minister of Finance)
content.text: Well, one of the proud achievements of this Government has been to deliver real tax relief to working people for the first time in 14 years, against the cries of Opposition. The Government inherited rapidly rising debt, persistent deficits, and high levels of spending. Our main priority has been to get the books back in order. We’ve been very disciplined with Government spending so that our fiscal repair job has not required new taxes, but it’s more than that. While getting the books back in order, we’ve also made significant tax changes that let people keep more of their own money, increasing support for working families and giving businesses an incentive to invest in productive assets that will grow the economy.

content.speaker: Ryan Hamilton
content.text: What personal tax policies has the Government introduced?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLA WILLIS
content.text: In 2024, the Government increased personal income tax thresholds and expanded eligibility for the independent earner tax credit. The effect of these changes was to deliver the first personal income tax relief for 14 years, and that tax relief went to working people. The Government also increased support for low to middle income working families, who got up to an extra $50 a fortnight, and we introduced FamilyBoost to help families with young children meet the costs of early childhood education. This was achieved within an overall operating package of $3.2 billion, which was significantly lower than recent Budgets under the previous Government. We managed to do a lot more for Kiwis’ back pockets through tax relief than the previous Government ever did.

content.speaker: Ryan Hamilton
content.text: What business tax policies has the Government introduced?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLA WILLIS
content.text: Well, the Government restored interest deductibility for residential rental property, returning to the normal practice of taxing profit, not revenue. While there were doubters, they have latterly had a road to Damascus experience on this one and recognised the value of this policy. In 2025, the Government introduced Investment Boost to encourage New Zealand businesses to make productive investments. It allows firms to immediately deduct 20 percent of the cost of a new asset, and this, of course, is an incentive to invest in machinery, tools, farm equipment, vehicles, industrial buildings, and other productive assets. Officials advised that this would increase productivity and lead to higher wages and higher employment, and, boy oh boy, the feedback from those who have used it is strong and positive.

content.speaker: Ryan Hamilton
content.text: What is the alternative to this approach?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLA WILLIS
content.text: Right now, people are very seriously proposing a capital gains tax. In fact, the Council of Trade Unions (CTU) in particular are promoting a comprehensive capital gains tax. I note that there are members of the CTU who are also prominently running in election seats this election. There are also people proposing a wealth tax, an inheritance tax, a gift tax, higher income tax rates, an increase in the company tax, a tax on profits sent offshore—a land tax removing interest deductibility for rental properties remains popular with some members of this House as a proposal—a 10-year brightline test, a vacant house tax, a stamp duty on residential sales, scrapping Investment Boost, and no GST on kai—those are all from parties over there. That hotchpotch, that potpourri of extra taxes, is the alternative.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: That’s it—OK.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLA WILLIS
content.text: We say no new taxes.
Prime Minister
Question No. 2

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRIS HIPKINS
content.text: Before I begin my question, I do want to acknowledge that it is our last question time before the election so therefore the last question time you’ll be presiding over before the election. I would like to take a moment to thank you for your good grace and your good humour in chairing question time in this term of Parliament. I hope that will continue for just a few more minutes.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Thanks very much. Take an extra supp!

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRIS HIPKINS (Leader of the Opposition)
content.text: to the Prime Minister: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON (Prime Minister)
content.text: Well, I want to join with the Leader of the Opposition and say thank you very much for your fantastic work, and I’d be quite happy for him to have an extra supp anyway. Look, the answer is yes, and I just want to reassure the member that we won’t be introducing a comprehensive capital gains tax, as proposed by Craig Renney on the Labour Party policy committee, a candidate, and also the Council of Trade Unions.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
content.text: Which economic record is he most proud of: real wages going backwards, GDP per capita being lower than when he became Prime Minister, or unemployment reaching a 14-year high?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: Actually, I’m really proud of the fact that we’ve delivered 2.6 percent GDP growth, which is higher than the US, Canada, the UK, EU, Japan, and Australia, for that matter. I’m really proud of the fact that we see our manufacturing sector going from strength to strength and the highest it’s been since 2021. I’m really proud of the services returning to expansion, record exports up $20 billion, tourism visitors back behind pre-COVID levels. We’ve got wholesale electricity prices coming down 35 percent, which is fantastic, and we’ve got consumer confidence, business, farmer confidence, and retail investor confidence at really good levels. We’re making progress. We’re really excited to kick on and carry on in a second term and get the rest of the job done for New Zealanders.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
content.text: Does he acknowledge that Kiwi households struggling to pay for their electricity bill will take no comfort from the idea that wholesale electricity prices have been falling when their own power bills have increased 20 percent under his leadership?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: What I can reassure Kiwis is that they take no comfort that the Labour-Greens Government ended oil and gas and drove up wholesale electricity prices and people lost their jobs. Low and middle income working New Zealanders across regional New Zealand lost their jobs because of very poor energy policy. I’m pleased with the fact that we have sorted it out in two and half years. We’ve done a great job.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
content.text: Is he still laser-focused on the cost of living, given the price of butter is up 71 percent under his leadership; bread, 65 percent; mince, 36 percent—all prices going up since he became Prime Minister—or does he just say to New Zealanders struggling with the cost of living, as he did in the House last week, “cry me a river”?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: No. What I’d say to New Zealanders about the cost of living is that you sure as hell don’t want any tax increases. That’s what actually takes money out of their pockets and puts it into a Labour - Greens - Te Pāti Māori - Opportunity coalition, which would be an absolute nightmare for this country. But for the member—I want to reassure him—tomatoes are down 29 percent, eggs are down 16 percent, lettuce is down 15 percent, chicken is down 4 percent. As I said to him last week, he’s more than welcome to go create a chicken parmigiana up at the bach a bit further north.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
content.text: Which of the following actions that his Government has taken does he think have helped Kiwis most with the rising cost of living: real-term cuts to the minimum wage three years in a row, cancelling pay equity for thousands of Kiwi women across the country, or scrapping fair pay agreements which would have raised the incomes of a lot of low-income Kiwis?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: The thing that makes the big difference is economic growth at 2.6 percent, because what that means is that we’re growing faster than many other countries around the world. We’re seeing our sectors start to fire up. That creates jobs and opportunities. What we have done is control spending and stop the dumb and wasteful stuff that we saw from the previous administration that drove up spending 70 percent. We’ve brought inflation back down from 7.2 percent—a 32-year high outside the band for three years. Twelve interest rate rises—we’ve got interest rates down, we’ve got the economy growing, and employment is coming.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
content.text: Which does he think has helped young Kiwis the most: cutting the Apprenticeship Boost programme, increasing student fees by almost 20 percent, or cutting financial support to 18- and 19-year-olds who can’t find work?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: I’d just say to any 18- or 19-year-old out there that we need 2,500 people in our defence forces—we’d really welcome applications there over the next few years. We need more police officers—there’s jobs going there too. But I’d just say to you, if you’re a young person in New Zealand, what you want to see is actually economic growth. That’s the important thing—2.6 percent is really great. That’s going to create 220,000 new jobs in the next four years, wages higher than inflation, and an economy growing at 2.7 percent on average each and every year.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
content.text: Which of his Government’s policies does he think has contributed the most to the record homelessness New Zealand’s currently experiencing: cancelling 3,500 new State houses, selling off over 1,000 State houses, or booting people out of emergency accommodation?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: I’d just say to the member, Labour used to care about housing, didn’t they? That’s what they used to care about, but, actually, we’ve made house pricing the most affordable it’s been in a long time. We have a record number of first-home buyers, running at 29 percent, and we have the most stable rent environment we’ve had in over 25 years. We come back to Government, and we find the State house wait-list has gone from 6,500 up to 24,000 or something. We’ve taken 6,000 off that list, and we’ve actually made rents go low. We have—yeah, we have. The wait-list is down. You don’t like to hear it, but that’s the reality of it, and we ended the scourge of motels and emergency housing—we stopped that—and we put a big investment into homelessness, and there are some good signs there too.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
content.text: What does he think has most improved health outcomes for New Zealanders: a hiring freeze that’s seen just 54 new nurses hired by our health system in the last two years, making it more expensive to fill prescriptions, or giving a $300 million tax break to the tobacco lobby?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: I’d just say to the member, isn’t it interesting. All they did in six years was actually introduce a Māori Health Authority and restructure the district health boards, and you didn’t give a toss about patient outcomes, and every single one of them went backwards. But isn’t it great; go look at the PR this morning because every health metric is on the up, and that’s thanks to the great work of Simeon Brown and Shane Reti, doing a brilliant, brilliant job focusing on patients rather than just tweaking and restructuring and dicking around.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
content.text: Why did his Government give the fire and emergency board a pay rise, whilst cutting $50 million in funding for fire and emergency services and offering front-line firefighters nothing?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: We have a lot to do in that space, and, as you know, we’ve got a new chair on that board. That board needs serious overhauling. They need to be able to get much more efficiency out of that corporate head office function, which was built up under his previous Government, and we have a package that, as I said, we announced this morning, a National policy on firefighters. It’s a good policy, and we’ve got work to do on that in the next term.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
content.text: Does the Prime Minister consider that, after 34 months lambasting “tax cuts for landlords” only to adopt that policy, that perhaps Peter Fraser’s party of principle has become Chris Hipkins’ party of plagiarism?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: I think the Minister raises a very good point—

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: No, no, no. There’ll be no answer there.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
content.text: Which statement does he think best represents his view of New Zealand and New Zealanders: calling low-income Kiwis “bottom feeders”, saying Kiwi businesses have a “parent-child mentality”, calling Kiwi small businesses “C-listers”, or saying that Kiwis are “wet, whiny, and inward-looking”?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: I’ve got to say to the member, this is an awesome country, this is the best country on planet Earth, and we are setting up this country for the future, because we’re doing the serious reforms as well as fixing the basics that Labour broke. I want to say I’m very proud of the policy going forward. New Zealand’s going to have a great future in this country because we’ve got a growing economy; we’ve got our communities safe in their homes, their businesses, and their communities; we’ve got a world-class education system emerging; and we’re improving health outcomes for New Zealanders.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
content.text: Which of the following statements by his own Ministers best represents his Government’s attitude towards migrant New Zealanders, given none of them received any sanction from him as Prime Minister: likening Indian Kiwis to a “butter chicken tsunami”, calling Chinese Kiwis “liars”, telling Mexican New Zealanders to “go home”, or telling a Cook Island New Zealander that “they aren’t really a New Zealander”?

content.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
content.text: Point of order. Mr Speaker, that statement made by Chris Hipkins is utterly false, as is—[Interruption] Listen up, you might learn something.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Hang on, just a moment. Points of order are heard in silence.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
content.text: —as is the very statement just made in the last few hours by that member of Parliament over there, who’s disowned what they’ve claimed to be the case. He said that the media got it entirely wrong as to what Winston Peters said. He made that statement. Why doesn’t that Minister know about it?

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Well, the—[Interruption]

content.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
content.text: Not a Minister yet, but will be in a few weeks.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Hang on, hang on. The point is definitely made, but the questioner was asking the Prime Minister’s views on various statements not attributed to anybody, so I think—

content.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
content.text: No, no he attributed it to me.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: No, he didn’t. [Interruption] Hang on a minute!

content.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
content.text: I put my hand up.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: What are you putting your hand up for? That’s the first time he’s ever asked permission for anything. Just ask the question again.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
content.text: Which of the following statements by his Ministers best reflects his Government’s attitude towards migrant New Zealanders, given none of them received any sanction from him as Prime Minister: likening Indian Kiwis to a butter chicken tsunami, calling Chinese Kiwis liars, telling Mexican New Zealanders to go home, or telling a Cook Island Kiwi that they aren’t really a New Zealander?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: Well I’m incredibly proud of our migrant community here in New Zealand. I think they’ve added to New Zealand, they’ve made it an infinitely better place. They leave everything behind, they come here, they work incredibly hard, they don’t go on welfare, they get their kids educated, they take one, two, three jobs to get a deposit for a business, and they are a great example to many New Zealanders to follow. But also, this is a Government that has ensured we have a smart, fair, targeted immigration system: we have made sure that we have moved it from 70 percent low-skill, to 70 percent high-skill. Net migration has gone from 135,000 down to 25,000, and we link our immigration policy to our economic agenda, and where our job skills and shortages are, as well as to our infrastructure growth and development. That’s the way in which we maintain a good buy-in for immigration in New Zealand.

content.speaker: Hon Chris Bishop
content.text: Would he support a member of his Government taking real estate data, going through the names, working out ones that sound Chinese, releasing that data in order to castigate a particular community and blame them for high house prices?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: No, I’d encourage the member to stand up for that too.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
content.text: What would he like his term as Prime Minister to be most remembered for: higher unemployment; real wages going backwards; higher food, electricity and fuel prices; a health system descending further into crisis; a shrinking economy; businesses going broke; or record number of Kiwis giving up and leaving New Zealand?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: I’d like our Government to be remembered for cleaning up Labour’s mess. That’s what we did. We have the economy growing, we have a much safer environment because we restored law and order, we’re building a world-class education system, and we’re improving healthcare. That’s what Kiwi’s want. They know that is what this Government has done. I would proudly put my record up against his record any day of the week, and I’m really looking forward to it, son, in the next six weeks.
Prime Minister
Question No. 3

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Question No. 2, Rawiri Waititi.

content.speaker: RAWIRI WAITITI
content.text: No. 3, Mr Speaker.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Oh, No. 3? Okay, sorry that last one was so long I’ve lost my way.

content.speaker: RAWIRI WAITITI
content.text: I was just in the spirit of the House. I also just want to acknowledge the stellar job you have done to facilitate this rowdy House at times. [Interruption]

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Sorry, can we please hear this in silence?

content.speaker: Hon Members
content.text: Ha, ha!

content.speaker: RAWIRI WAITITI
content.text: For the sake of an extra supplementary—for your grace.

content.speaker: Hon Members
content.text: Ha, ha!

content.speaker: RAWIRI WAITITI (Co-Leader—Te Pāti Māori)
content.text: to the Prime Minister: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions in relation to improving outcomes for Māori?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON (Prime Minister)
content.text: Absolutely.

content.speaker: Rawiri Waititi
content.text: Why does the Prime Minister define success for Māori by counting how many Māori he has kicked out of emergency housing, how many Māori he has put into prison, and how many parents have been prosecuted to address attendance, rather than whether Māori have secure homes, decent incomes, good health, access to Māori-medium education, and genuine control over our own futures?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: As I have said to the member repeatedly, we don’t believe in histrionics and performative stuff; we actually get things done in this Government. Just think about it: 18 Treaty Settlements advanced; a thousand-plus Māori families out of emergency housing, 80 percent reduction; Māori health provider funding nearly doubled over this Government. I could go on.

content.speaker: Rawiri Waititi
content.text: Does he deny that good process leads to good outcomes; and if not, does he consider that his Government’s removal of Māori authority across processes that impact Māori the most will only led to worse outcomes for Māori in the future?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: I reject the characterisation of that question. As I’ve said, Māori youth offending is down 28 percent. We have 4,000 fewer Māori victims of violent crime—that’s a good thing; I think the member would want to celebrate that, wouldn’t you?

content.speaker: Rawiri Waititi
content.text: On his last day, will the PM take responsibility or just his belongings?

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: I didn’t hear that. Will what?

content.speaker: Rawiri Waititi
content.text: Would you like me to repeat it? On his last day, will the PM take responsibility or just take his belongings?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: Well, I take responsibility for the outcomes that we’ve improved for Māori. Tamariki Māori immunised at 24 months has gone up from 60 percent to 71.3 percent. I just find it unusual that the member who purports to advocate for Māori doesn’t care about outcomes and improving their daily life. We do, on this side—Māori, non-Māori.
RMA Reform
Question No. 4

content.speaker: Dr HAMISH CAMPBELL (National—Ilam)
content.text: to the Minister responsible for RMA Reform: What recent milestones have been achieved in the Government’s work to replace the Resource Management Act 1991?

content.speaker: Hon CHRIS BISHOP (Minister responsible for RMA Reform)
content.text: As of around 9.45 p.m. last night, the Resource Management Act (RMA) has been repealed. After 35 years of the RMA being a millstone around the neck of this country, we’ve now passed legislation for a fundamentally different way of planning for New Zealand’s future, as I think there is widespread consensus in the Parliament that the RMA has made it slower, harder, and more expensive to build homes, infrastructure, grow the food, and build the energy we rely on. It’s failed to prevent environmental degradation; we’ve had the worst of both worlds. We now have a new system—narrower, simpler, faster, more consistent, more upfront about the trade-offs we need to make, to make sure that as a country we can grow and thrive.

content.speaker: Dr Hamish Campbell
content.text: What are the key changes that have been made as part of these reforms?

content.speaker: Hon CHRIS BISHOP
content.text: Unlike the RMA, most of the big decisions we made more upfront in the legislation and upfront in the system. It means we can stop relitigating the same questions over and over again through individual consent applications. One hundred planning documents will be replaced by 17 regional combined plans; we’ll have nationally standardised zones and rules to reduce variation across the country. Officials estimate around 45 percent of consent and permit applications currently required under the RMA could be removed under the new system. The economic benefits of these reforms are significant. Independent analysis projects the new planning system will boost GDP by an additional 0.56 percent every year by 2050, worth up to $3.1 billion annually. These are fundamentally good reforms to supercharge our economy.

content.speaker: Dr Hamish Campbell
content.text: How important is the implementation of the new planning system going to be to its success?

content.speaker: Hon CHRIS BISHOP
content.text: Passing the legislation is a significant achievement for the Government, but the hard work is just beginning. When Parliament passed the RMA in 1991, it was assumed that there would be a whole lot of extra work done after that, which never happened, so the Government is very focused on the implementation around spatial planning, around national direction, and around national standards over the next two to three years. We’re also focused on driving a culture change in the new system. The RMA encouraged a culture focused on process, repeated litigation, development treated as something to be constrained not enabled. We’re working hard at changing the incentives and we’re investing in implementation. Budget 2026 invested $294 million over four years to support the roll-out of our new planning system; more will be required but we are getting on with the job.

content.speaker: Dr Hamish Campbell
content.text: What do the Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill do for New Zealand’s future?

content.speaker: Hon CHRIS BISHOP
content.text: One of the things that I have been reflecting on over the last three years is that we are not as wealthy as a country as sometimes we think we are, and we are certainly nowhere near as prosperous as we should be. We are, indeed, at a crossroads. We can accept a low-growth past, present, and future; we can continue to be a relatively poor country, and the continued degradation of our natural environment, or we can take tough choices and make hard decisions. If we get it right, it means our children can access higher living standards, better education, better healthcare systems, and protect the natural environment. The RMA reforms that this Government has implemented represent tough decisions in the national interest to set New Zealand up for success in the 2030s. They are part of this Government’s plan to build the future.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
content.text: Can the Minister point to just one single fast-track consent application for developing industry that the dancing tussocks in the Greens have supported?

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: No, look, you can’t make that—if he wants to, reword your question. Do you want to ask the question again without reference to a particular style of Government?

content.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
content.text: You mean about the “tussocks”?

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: As it happens.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
content.text: OK, then. Can the Minister point to just one single fast-track consent application for developing industry that the Greens have supported?

content.speaker: Hon CHRIS BISHOP
content.text: Well, I’ve struggled. There have been 35 fast-track applications that have now been approved, including projects that I think most people would say are pretty good. The first hydro scheme consented in New Zealand in a long time on the West Coast, Waitaha hydro; new solar, new wind farms, green steel—recycled steel proposal; development of aquaculture by iwi. Many, many projects; 990 megawatts of new renewable energy just in the last year alone. Sadly, the Greens have supported none of those projects.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Yeah, good—good. He asked for one.
Finance
Question No. 5

content.speaker: Hon BARBARA EDMONDS (Labour—Mana)
content.text: to the Minister of Finance: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLA WILLIS (Minister of Finance)
content.text: In context, yes, and I am advised by the Parliamentary Library that this is the 51st time in this parliamentary term that I’ve been asked that exact question by the member, and not once have I resiled from my commitment to lower taxes for working people.

content.speaker: Hon Barbara Edmonds
content.text: Dramatic. Is the total number of KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals better or worse since she became Minister of Finance?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLA WILLIS
content.text: Well, since I became Minister of Finance, people’s default contributions to their KiwiSaver funds have increased, as have the contributions that match those from their employers. This will have a material effect on the size of people’s nest eggs in the years ahead, and I am proud of that. It is also the case that, while I have been Minister of Finance, this economy has been going through an extremely difficult recovery, which is reflected in the KiwiSaver stats that the member refers to. I recommend the member a report put out yesterday from independent experts that says, in part, the difficult recovery in New Zealand has experienced was exacerbated by poor decision-making by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, enabled through the loosening of guard rails from the last Government that allowed it to take its eye off the inflation-busting ball, and it’s led to higher unemployment and slower growth than would have otherwise been the case. More Kiwis would be in work right now if you hadn’t mucked up the Reserve Bank’s job.

content.speaker: Hon Barbara Edmonds
content.text: Is the number of homeless New Zealanders better or worse since she became Minister of Finance?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLA WILLIS
content.text: Well, that will depend on which survey you refer to. But I stood in this House in Opposition and lamented that children were being raised in gross motel rooms, and we committed that we would fix that. I am extraordinarily proud that this Government, through its prioritisation of families who were otherwise condemned to live in motel rooms, has put them into warm, dry, social homes, because I don’t think kids should be raised in emergency motel rooms. [Interruption]

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Just one person asking a question.

content.speaker: Hon Barbara Edmonds
content.text: Is the number of children living in material hardship better or worse since she became Minister of Finance?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLA WILLIS
content.text: We have published a child poverty report with each Budget, and one of the things that that shows is that when you deliver income tax relief to working people, that improves the conditions—the material conditions—in which parents can raise their children. It matters if people can keep more of what they earn, and it matters when they can get a FamilyBoost tax credit for their early childhood fees, and it matters when the Government spends their money carefully so it can keep taxes low.

content.speaker: Hon Barbara Edmonds
content.text: If the number of KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals, the number of New Zealanders unemployed, the number of businesses liquidated, the number of people who are homeless, the number of children in material hardship, real wages, GDP per capita, and the cost of living are all worse since she became the Minister of Finance, are her chances of getting back into Parliament better or worse?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLA WILLIS
content.text: Well, given that member’s sole suggestion for addressing the cost of living crisis for the past three years has been “We wouldn’t have done tax cuts for landlords,” and now she’s changed her mind, I’d say to you: we’ve delivered on our plan, we’ve delivered on our commitments, we have fixed the basics, and we are building the future. You got nothing.
Regulation
Question No. 6

content.speaker: TODD STEPHENSON (ACT)
content.text: to the Minister for Regulation: What actions has the Government taken to reduce regulation for New Zealanders?

content.speaker: Hon DAVID SEYMOUR (Minister for Regulation)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker, and in keeping with other party leaders, I’d like to thank you for your grace and forbearance in trying to manage this place over the last three years. I begin my answer to the question by saying that this Government, I believe, will be looked back on as a Government where New Zealand started to turn the corner on regulation. The establishment of the Ministry for Regulation and the Regulatory Standards Act are some of the institutions that we’ve created, and they have saved hundreds of millions of dollars already. However, the changes that the House voted through last night to replace the Resource Management Act with two new laws based on property rights—that will halve the number of consents required for the same amount of activity; that will add half a percent or about $3 billion a year to GDP—that is the largest, most significant change that this Government has made, and yet it is far from the only one in this Government of deregulation.

content.speaker: Todd Stephenson
content.text: What has the Government done to reduce unnecessary regulation in health?

content.speaker: Hon DAVID SEYMOUR
content.text: Many things on the health front—for example, 12-month prescriptions up from three, allowing Kiwis, particularly those managing chronic health conditions, to save time and money. Medsafe introduced the rule of two, something that all three coalition parties campaigned on. Now if a medicine has been consented in two other developed countries in the last four years, it will be available and consented here within 30 days. We’ve also aligned over the counter labelling requirements with Australia so more over the counter medicines can be sold here at better prices, with more choice. But perhaps most significantly, we have legalised pseudoephedrine to wake you up and melatonin to put you back to sleep.

content.speaker: Hon Andrew Hoggard
content.text: What has the Government done to cut red tape for farmers?

content.speaker: Hon DAVID SEYMOUR
content.text: Well, I have in the back of my mind your recent admonishments for excessively long answers, so I’ll give only a sample. The Agricultural and Horticultural Products Regulatory Review has dramatically reduced the queues for new products being consented in New Zealand, and that gives farmers more affordable and more environmentally friendly agricultural compounds, veterinary medicines, and the like that allow them to compete with the rest of the world. That is a very good example of deregulation, as are Andrew Hoggard’s simpler, risk-based freshwater farm plans, and we are currently ensuring that New Zealand farmers will be able to use drones more easily as the modern flying tractor of the innovative Kiwi farm.

content.speaker: Laura McClure
content.text: What has the Government done to cut red tape in education?

content.speaker: Hon DAVID SEYMOUR
content.text: Again, many things. The sector review of the early childhood education sector is estimated to save $40 million in compliance costs while ramping up the focus on child safety, with a new proportional approach to regulation, a new regulator, and a much more constructive relationship between the regulator and the regulated. The Government has also introduced charter schools, which increase the choice and allow those who have innovative ways to educate young New Zealanders and help unlock their potential to teach and educate their way. The change that is making and the potential being unlocked in young New Zealanders up and down this country at over 20 charter schools now is absolutely touching and perhaps the thing that I, in politics, am most proud of.

content.speaker: Hon Nicole McKee
content.text: What has the Government done to reduce red tape for the hospitality sector?

content.speaker: Hon DAVID SEYMOUR
content.text: No sector has been left untouched, nearly. The hospitality sector has had a very hard row to hoe in recent years. The first was lockdown, then being told they could open the next day by a Government that didn’t understand that they hadn’t actually had time to order the food to serve that day, then a prolonged cost of living crisis in recession. This Government has relieved the regulatory pressure on them. For example, the Minister who asked the question has ensured that if you want to object to a liquor licence, you actually have to live in the community and be affected by it. You can’t object from another country. We will be rolling out, over the next half-year to a year, simpler food-control plans that are proportionate to risk, allowing venues to put up marquees more easily through the Building Act, and letting venues charge for courtesy shuttles to bring down drink-driving. In every way, we are making it easier to run a hospitality venue, by removing red tape and regulation. Nobody had listened to them for a long time, perhaps ever, until the Ministry for Regulation came along and gave them an intelligent, sympathetic ear, and it turned into action.

content.speaker: Hon Karen Chhour
content.text: What regulations has the Government changed to improve access to healthcare for children in care?

content.speaker: Hon DAVID SEYMOUR
content.text: I have to commend the member, who’s visited every single Oranga Tamariki facility and overseen significant improvements in safety in those facilities for some of the most vulnerable children—and she’s done it without a single bucket of KFC to get anyone off the roof. She’s also deregulated by letting trained, authorised staff administer emergency medicines like EpiPens, and by letting nurse practitioners carry out health exams so those vulnerable children are more likely to get the healthcare they need.

content.speaker: Cameron Luxton
content.text: What has the Government done to make it easier to build homes?

content.speaker: Hon DAVID SEYMOUR
content.text: Many, many things. For too long, it’s been too hard to build a home, too hard to build a whare on your whenua. We have, for example, allowed recognised building materials—certified in trusted overseas schemes, including 128,000 Australian WaterMark products—to be used here. We’re letting plumbers and drainlayers self-certify; we’ve reformed the rushed earthquake laws, that I have to say only one member of this House voted against; we’re now saving $9 billion in regulatory relief there. We have got rid of the joint and several liability that meant that councils were so unwilling to say yes to construction. Furthermore—slightly tangential to regulation—we have introduced revenue sharing between central and local government, so councils have an incentive to say yes to growth.

content.speaker: Dr Parmjeet Parmar
content.text: Supplementary, Mr Speaker.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: No, I think we’re all done.

content.speaker: Hon David Seymour
content.text: Point of order, Mr Speaker. I seek leave for the ACT Party to have one more supplementary question so the people of New Zealand can learn about the enormous progress made by this Government of deregulation.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Is there any objection? There is. The Hon Marama Davidson.
Prime Minister
Question No. 7

content.speaker: Hon MARAMA DAVIDSON
content.text: And what a fine Speaker you have been, Mr Speaker—the leadership, the guaranteed entertainment. I dressed up especially for you, Mr Speaker, and I’m always in the market for extra supplementaries. Thank you, Mr Speaker.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: See how you go!

content.speaker: Hon MARAMA DAVIDSON (Co-Leader—Green)
content.text: to the Prime Minister: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
[Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?]

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON (Prime Minister)
content.text: Yes, and in particular, our desire never to introduce a 45 percent top tax rate, never to introduce a death or inheritance tax, a gift tax, a rentals tax, or a wealth asset tax.

content.speaker: Hon Marama Davidson
content.text: Whose interests was he serving when he amended his resource management reforms to reflect the demands of corporate lobby groups?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: Well, we didn’t do that, as we have discussed previously.

content.speaker: Hon Marama Davidson
content.text: Whose interests was he serving when he cut funding for Predator Free, passed a bill legalising the killing of kiwi, and cut protections for fresh water?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: I reject the characterisation of that question.

content.speaker: Hon Marama Davidson
content.text: Whose interests was he serving when he weakened our climate targets, disestablished the Ministry for the Environment, and cancelled plans to electrify our transport fleet?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: Actually, I’m quite proud of the fact that we had 96.4 percent renewable energy in the last quarter. I’m quite proud of the fact that we’ve built more renewable projects in the last two years than the previous eight years, and I’m actually proud of the fact that we’ve had the lowest level of emissions from our economy, since records began in 2010, in the last quarter as well.

content.speaker: Hon Marama Davidson
content.text: What is his message to the tens of thousands of New Zealanders who took to the streets in Auckland on Saturday, marching to demand environmental protections, who now see his Government dismantling decades of environmental protections?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: I disagree. They’ve actually got a Government that will ensure the environment is protected, but, most importantly, they will grow and they will have jobs and opportunities for them and their families.

content.speaker: Hon Marama Davidson
content.text: How are we going, Mr Speaker? Can I have one more? Thank you. Was he serving the interests of the New Zealand public when he decided to subsidise oil and gas, fast-track mining applications, and make it easier to mine in and around significant biodiversity and wetlands?

content.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
content.text: We are very, very proud of having reversed the oil and gas ban. That was, single-handedly, a point of absolute insanity from the last Government. That led to higher electricity prices and higher power bills, and we have a very comprehensive energy strategy that is working. We are proud of accelerating a renewables boom, and we’re also proud of having the thermal firming energy we need to keep prices low in a dry year.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Question No. 8, Dr Ayesha Verrall—the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall.
Health
Question No. 8

content.speaker: Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour)
content.text: to the Minister of Health: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I’m not going ask for extra supplementaries, but I am always on the lookout for good answers. My question is to the Minister of Health: Does he stand by his statement that the health system is “finally turning a corner”; if so, why?

content.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN (Minister of Health)
content.text: Well, Mr Speaker, thank you so much for your leadership of this Parliament. I just want to add my congratulations, alongside everyone else, before I answer my question. In the context it was made, yes. This morning, I announced the most recent health targets results, covering April to June, showing significant improvement across all five health targets. All five health targets are set for 2030, and every one has now improved for two years running, which is the steady, year-on-year progress needed to reach the 2030 targets. Key improvements include more than 14,000 fewer patients waiting more than four months since the peak, a reduction of 41 percent; shorter waits for elective treatment in every district across the country, including a 21 percentage point improvement in Whanganui, a 14 percentage point improvement in Gisborne, and a 10 percentage point improvement in South Canterbury; continued improvement in immunisation rates; faster cancer treatment; and shorter stays in emergency departments, particularly compared to 2023, when that member was the Minister of Health. We know there is more work to do, and that is exactly why now is the time to double down on the health targets and not return to removing them, like Labour did in 2017, and to make sure that we continue the progress that our hard-working front-line staff are delivering across the country.

content.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
content.text: Can he confirm that Middlemore’s emergency department has routinely operated at 200 percent over capacity and that staff are being asked to come to work when sick?

content.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
content.text: According to the emergency department target data that was released today, in the most recent quarter, Middlemore Hospital improved from 65 percent to 76.9 percent of patients being seen within six hours. That is one of the highest, best improvements of any hospital up and down this country, and that member should be proud of the great work being done by the front-line staff at that hospital.

content.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
content.text: Can he confirm that in Waikato, his Government has cut staff by 90 fulltime-equivalent nurses over the past year?

content.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
content.text: I want to point out the most recent quarterly data on emergency departments, which shows that improvements at the Waikato district health board—69.3 percent, up to 73.8 percent of patients seen within six hours at the hospital. There are shorter wait-times for elective treatment, from 74.2 percent seen within four months, up to 80.6 percent—above the milestone. That is thanks to the hard-working front-line staff at Waikato Hospital.

content.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
content.text: Can he confirm that in Christchurch emergency department, 15,000 patients were treated in corridors last year, nearly four times more than in 2023?

content.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
content.text: We’ve got more good news, and if you look at the most recent health targets report, shorter wait-times for elective treatment at Canterbury has improved from 62.9 percent of patients seen within four months, up to 71.4 percent seen within four months. What about first specialist appointments? 50.8 percent seen within four months last quarter, up to 57.7 percent. The member opposite might like to talk down our health system, but we are seeing year-on-year improvements under this Government, after decline under her watch.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
content.text: Does the Minister of Health consider that had qualified doctors and nurses not been mandated out of their jobs by the previous Government, leading to permanent employment scarring, that New Zealand would have more trained professionals in our hospitals, GP offices, and healthcare centres?

content.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
content.text: Our focus has been to grow the number of front-line staff across our health system. We have 900 additional doctors working at Health New Zealand since we’ve come to Government. We are training more at the University of Auckland and Otago; with a third medical school that this Government is funding and building—that Labour opposed. We’re supporting our front-line nursing workforce with 2,100 more nurses working at Health New Zealand since we came to Government. We’re investing in nurses in primary care, with nurses becoming nurse practitioners. This Government is backing our front-line health workforce, while Labour continues to talk it down.

content.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
content.text: Is he really content to leave his last comment in this Parliament, on the matter of 15,000 people in Christchurch Hospital waiting in corridors, to be, “More good news”?

content.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
content.text: There is more work to do. Every time I’m asked about our healthcare system, I acknowledge there is huge amount more work to do. But after six years of decline under the previous Government, six years of decline in our emergency departments under the previous Government, things are on the way up. Improving under National; down under Labour. Let’s not go back to what they did to our health system.
Education
Question No. 9

content.speaker: KATIE NIMON (National—Napier)
content.text: to the Minister of Education: What has she achieved in this term of Government?

content.speaker: Hon ERICA STANFORD (Minister of Education)
content.text: After decades of declining achievement, we’re a Government that’s putting raising achievement and closing the equity gap at the heart of everything we’re doing. We introduced an hour of reading, writing, and maths; we banned cellphones in schools; we’ve delivered every single curriculum area from years 1 to 13 for the New Zealand curriculum and Te Marautanga o Aotearoa; we’ve mandated the structured literacy teaching in every school in New Zealand; we’ve introduced structured maths; we’ve trained over 50,000 teachers in structured literacy and structured maths; we’ve funded maths books, science books, and music kits in every primary school in New Zealand in English and te reo Māori; and we’re scrapping NCEA and replacing it with meaningful qualifications to set kids up for success—and the results are starting to show.

content.speaker: Katie Nimon
content.text: What has she achieved in assessment and reporting to parents?

content.speaker: Hon ERICA STANFORD
content.text: For the first time in our country’s history, we have consistent nationwide mandated twice-yearly assessments between year 3 and year 8 to measure progress in reading, writing, and maths, to measure progress over time. We’ve delivered the 20 and 40 weeks phonics checks in English and te reo Māori; we’re delivering the Year 2 maths check in term 4 this year; and parents are, finally, receiving detailed reports on how their children are progressing and how they can help at home using our new Parent Portal tool. We are measuring progress consistently. We’re acting sooner and giving parents clearer information to raise achievement and close the equity gap.

content.speaker: Katie Nimon
content.text: What has she achieved in learning support?

content.speaker: Hon ERICA STANFORD
content.text: Budget 2025 was the largest injection into learning support in a generation, with three-quarters of a billion dollars. We’re delivering a learning support coordinator in every single primary and intermediate school in New Zealand—promised by that side and not delivered. We uncapped Ongoing and Reviewable Resourcing Scheme (ORRS) funding, with 1,057 extra children receiving ORRS support—uncapping ORRS funding: promised by that side, delivered by this side. We’ve funded the expansion of the Early Intervention Service, that saw over 6,000 year 1 students receive support this year to transition to school; a thousand extra placements have been made available for private providers to get children off wait-lists for specialist services; and we’ve taken 15.7 days off the average wait time for early intervention support—more children who need support are being seen sooner.

content.speaker: Katie Nimon
content.text: What has she achieved in school property?

content.speaker: Hon ERICA STANFORD
content.text: More good news. We’ve set up the New Zealand School Property Agency to drive better value for money and better response to schools. We’ve halved the cost of building a school classroom and put an end to open-plan classrooms; we’ve funded nearly 1,400 classrooms across the country in three years. We invested more than double the funding into property maintenance over Budget 2024 and 2025 than in the previous six years combined. We’ve raised five-year agreement individual school property and maintenance grants by 50 percent. We’ve funded three new specialist schools for the first time in 50 years; we’ve funded over 140 extra satellite classrooms for specialist schools; and we’ve funded 500 schools to have solar panels. We are delivering in school property.

content.speaker: Katie Nimon
content.text: What results has she seen on these reforms?

content.speaker: Hon ERICA STANFORD
content.text: We are finally, after decades of decline and stagnation, seeing results improve under this Government. The New Zealand Herald led with my favourite headline this year—“The Phonic Boom”—when, last year, we saw the number of children at expectation for early reading and writing go from 36 percent to 58 percent after just three terms. The 2025 Curriculum Insights data showed us that at year 6, the number of children at curriculum expectations for maths rose by 6 percent, and 5 percent for writing—the first time we’ve seen significant improvements for years. Our international Programme for International Student Assessment results showed that while the trend for the rest of the OECD was in decline, New Zealand held steady in maths and reading and improved in science. But, importantly, the equity gap closed for the first time. I want to take this opportunity to thank our principals and teachers for these achievements. Our plan to raise achievement and close the equity gap is working, and we cannot put this all at risk by returning to the low-aspiration, low-expectation, low-bar Labour.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Question No. 10, Arena Williams. [Interruption] Hang on a minute. Sorry. I’ve called it.

content.speaker: Hon Kieran McAnulty
content.text: It’s a two-way street, isn’t it.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: No, no, no. You’ve got to allow your member to ask the question she’s called to ask.

content.speaker: Hon Kieran McAnulty
content.text: She’s more than capable.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Yeah, she is, and that’s why she doesn’t need your assistance.
Commerce and Consumer Affairs
Question No. 10

content.speaker: ARENA WILLIAMS (Labour—Manurewa)
content.text: to the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs: Are New Zealanders paying more than they should for groceries; if so, does he agree that they should not have to wait for another review before the Government takes action?

content.speaker: Hon CAMERON BREWER (Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs)
content.text: Mr Speaker, if I’m nice to you, will you give them less supplementaries?

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: If this was a Government question, you wouldn’t be getting an answer at all!

content.speaker: Hon CAMERON BREWER
content.text: Yes, New Zealanders pay too much for groceries. That is why this Government has made it easier to build supermarkets, strengthened the grocery supply code and competition settings, and backed the Commerce Commission’s enforcement work. We also commissioned independent analysis of structural reform, and that independent analysis is now finished and public on the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) website. Of the options tested, separating Foodstuffs has the strongest case.

content.speaker: Arena Williams
content.text: Why should a family whose grocery bill is higher today than when National took office believe that their food will be more affordable under that plan, when all along he has been telling us that, under his Government, it will just get more expensive more slowly?

content.speaker: Hon CAMERON BREWER
content.text: Because, under this Government, our track record on inflation, food inflation included, stands for itself. In the last 12 months to July 2026, food inflation was just 1.9 percent. In the last 12 months of the previous Labour Government, food inflation for one year was 12.5 percent.

content.speaker: Arena Williams
content.text: Why, when even the Prime Minister acknowledges that supermarkets are already making excess profits, does he need another review to tell him if changes to the grocery sector are needed?

content.speaker: Hon CAMERON BREWER
content.text: We’re not doing another review. If the member was to look on MBIE’s website, it’s complete—it’s complete. Government’s commissioned independent analysis of structural options is finished and is public. The autonomous, independent Commerce Commission will then take—with all the intention in the world, after this election, when the mandate’s even bigger, ComCom will look at that and make up recommendations, and, in six months’ time, we’re back in business.

content.speaker: Arena Williams
content.text: Why has his Government spent $274,000 on a review of a review to tell him to break up the supermarkets, when he was too weak to get a supermarket break-up through Cabinet?

content.speaker: Hon CAMERON BREWER
content.text: I suppose the question could be put back: why consider, hypothetically, a wholesale retail split, when MBIE’s own commissioned independent analysis, and the Commerce Commission, outright ruled against a wholesale retail split?

content.speaker: Arena Williams
content.text: Point of order. I seek leave to table a document from MBIE dated 21 September 2026, obtained under the Official Information Act (OIA) but not publicly released, which details the cost of the review of the review.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: How’s it not publicly released if it’s obtained under the OIA?

content.speaker: Arena Williams
content.text: It was released only two days ago and is not available on MBIE’s website.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Leave is sought for that purpose. Is there any objection? There appears to be none.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

content.speaker: Arena Williams
content.text: Thank you. Why should Kiwis expect any better from a Government whose answer on food prices has been to tell Kiwis to be grateful for price increases of only 143 percent for the tomatoes and 31 percent for the cheese in the Prime Minister’s chicken parmigiana?

content.speaker: Hon CAMERON BREWER
content.text: Because, as I’ve said before, our record speaks for itself on food inflation.
