We are all united as New Zealanders who made that journey, and I’m proud that, in this Government, when two patients come in for pre-diabetic medicine, they both get the same treatment, based on their clinical need now, not treated differently, where one pays and the other doesn’t because one’s ancestors came here at a different time. It’s the same with bowel cancer screening.

content.speaker: Hon Carmel Sepuloni
content.text: Oh David, that is not right.

content.speaker: Hon DAVID SEYMOUR
content.text: Yes, that is right. That’s exactly what we’ve done. Carmel Sepuloni needs to keep up. Then you look at the Māori Health Authority, gone; three waters, no longer co-governed. This Government has brought about one law for all and one future together. Yes, we started a debate no one else had the courage to start, let alone follow through, on the true meaning of our Treaty. It cannot be the case that our founding document is the Treaty, that the Treaty divides us into a partnership between races, and that we are a liberal democratic society. You can have any two of those, but not all three at the same time. That is why the ACT Party will continue to campaign for one law for all, one future together, equal rights before the law as human beings, not discriminated against on the basis of when our ancestors arrived in this country.

This country has great potential; it has great hope. If we can ensure that the work of this coalition Government continues, that the streets remain safe because victims are the priority in the home, in the shop, and out in public; if we can ensure that the Government is smaller and more efficient—perhaps with 10 or 15 or 19 departments but far fewer than we have right now—and if we can ensure that we have a red tape jihad that frees people up to be more productive and spend less time in compliance activity; and if we can treat each other as New Zealanders, equal before the law, regardless of when we arrived, there is no limit to what we can achieve. There is no reason that we should not be the wealthiest country on Earth, and there is no reason we should not be proud to call New Zealand home, as the greatest society that humanity has ever known. Thank you, Mr Speaker.

content.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Minister of Foreign Affairs)
content.text: As this Parliament adjourns, it’s appropriate to record our thanks to the cleaners, the library staff, the security teams, Hansard staff, committee clerks, chauffeurs, receptionists, and every other worker in this House, including yourself, Mr Speaker, your deputy, and assistant speakers.

Now, adjournment debates are traditionally a time to outline a politician’s record in this House across the term of Parliament. Unlike others, we have the rare privilege of actually having a record. That is why we say thank you to Shane Jones, Casey Costello, Mark Patterson, Jenny Marcroft, and their teams supporting them in their Government portfolios and, indeed, to the entire New Zealand First caucus and our team.

We are a party limited by the Standing Orders to only four member’s bills at any one time, but we have introduced 56 private member’s bills in the last term—56. That means we’ve done the work, we’ve done the research, we’re not all talk—fast on the lip and slow on the hip—no, we do the actual work.

These bills represent—[Interruption]—no, you can cheer later; you can applaud later—new ideas in line with New Zealand First’s values of social conservatism, patriotism, economic nationalism, and common sense. Our bills will be ready to be adopted in the forthcoming coalition agreement, and members of our supporting governing parties will, no doubt, look forward to advancing the interests of the common man and woman in the next term of Parliament.

We cannot get too far ahead of ourselves, because there is much too much good news to share in our record of this term. When New Zealand First makes an agreement, we keep our word. We’re famous for it too. You need to not judge us only by our words but by our deeds. We said the regions needed investment. We invested $1.2 billion into the regional infrastructure fund—money directed into productive and resilient assets around this country. Jobs, jobs, and jobs and wealth created in New Zealand with training chances for our young people.

We said that the Therapeutic Products Act was the wrong law, overtly complicated, over-bureaucratic, and a threat to the natural health products sector. And it was repealed. We said young New Zealanders waiting for mental health assistance needed practical help right then with providers like Gumboot Friday. We kept our promise. By November last year, more than 40,000 counselling sessions had been delivered through the Gumboot Friday programme.

We said English, the international language of commerce and the language used overwhelmingly in this House—including by the Greens, on a good day—should have the same statutory recognition of its official status that other official languages have. On 7 August this year, that became the law.

We said New Zealanders were entitled to a wider examination of the country’s response to the COVID-19 occurrence and not a mark-your-own-homework exercise as happened under Labour. The expanded royal commission completed its work and delivered its final report in February this year. It found young people between 12 and 17 were given second doses when Chris Hipkins and Ayesha Verrall were told not to do that; 311,000 young people wrongly got the dose.

Labour were found scurrying amongst nurses and teachers—meaning training professionals who were desperately, desperately needed in hospitals and classrooms—and they sacked them. They mandated them out of a job. And then they get in this House every day and talk about a lack of nurses and doctors—hundreds and hundreds of which they sacked. The Opposition yells about the need for more teachers and nurses—well, shame on them for mandating them out of the profession.

We said our citizens deserved recognition and practical support. Budget 2026 funded the next generation of the SuperGold card, including the option of a free physical ID that seniors have long called for.

Then there is the question of the infrastructure. While others campaigned to get our country back on track, you need look no further than New Zealand First to get evidence of who actually delivered it—$1.075 billion for rail network funding in Budget 2026. This is the first time ever a full three-year programme has been funded in advance—not fiscal cliffs like under Labour.

On the Cook Strait: we fixed the ferries for road and rail, and we’re going to save $2.3 billion from the idiocy we inherited, where the ferries were going to cost 20 percent of the total cost. So you go to buy ferries and they spent 80 percent of the money on infrastructure. How foolish. Go look at Tasmania and see where that would have got us; $2.3 billion saved—

content.speaker: Hon Rachel Brooking
content.text: Government by text message—what a shameful way to govern!

content.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
content.text: Don’t argue about the common sense of this. I know you’re slow. Can I ask you this question: what’s your business background? What’s your business background?

content.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
content.text: Zero!

content.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
content.text: Zero—exactly. It ain’t hard to get it right when you have experience—unlike the last lot who pursued palatial department allowances and wanted to lift the arts so high that Noah could berth his ark. When the fuel crisis hit our shores, who ensured we finally sorted out increased storage at Marsden Point by nine days, just like that? That’s right, it was New Zealand First.

Likewise, this House has finally grappled with the 1980s misadventure of the legal fraternity to invent Treaty principles. Now, I know imitation’s the most sincere form of flattery, but how many people now agree with us? Māori leaders like Ngata, Pōmare, Buck, and Carroll all understood the Treaty was a pact between two peoples to create one nation, one people under one flag and with one name. They understood the Treaty has no principles in it. This country has had it up to here with the wah-wah-wānanga delivering nothing but grievance founded on spurious words invented by the Labour Party. The country respects the Treaty signed in 1840—not the made-up nonsense written in those 1980s university clubhouses. That is why we have repealed those provisions with certain legislation—and we have more work ahead of us.

That is what it looks like to understand reality. We know what a Treaty is; we know what a woman is—[Interruption]. Oh, it’s got them going. One more time: we know what a woman is—hush for a while—and we know what realpolitik looks like in foreign affairs. We’ve got the experience; the others are all talk.

In our efforts, we have spent eight months abroad rebuilding New Zealand’s relationship with the world, including visiting all 17 Pacific member States and China—yes, I’ve been to China, not once but twice. Yes, I have a great relationship with China. Of course, I was the first guy to ever have a business connection with China when I did the export education in 1997—the first deal ever; you’ve all forgotten. So we’ve been offshore for eight months.

But, look, we’ve spent more time in this House than every Māori Party MP combined, including the two who got chucked out. Now, tell me, what on earth is going on in the mainstream media when I have to tell you that information? All this time, since 1867, the law was changed to accept Māori into this Parliament and they don’t turn up, for the first time ever.

Members, there is much more work ahead to fix this country. To govern a country, you need to know the ropes. The world is tough out there in reality and away from the cloistered comfort of the Green and Labour Party MPs in the leafy suburbs.

We are the party who ensured the minimum wage, who lifted and strengthened the fast-track legislation to enable industry to create jobs for our own, and who knows what hard work looks like. New Zealanders are sick and tired of globalist ideologies capturing politicians and leading to industry closing down and people losing their jobs—

content.speaker: Hon Member
content.text: Tell us about the gays, Winston!

content.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
content.text: Look, come to Tauranga on Saturday afternoon at 2 o’clock to Trinity—it’ll be wall to wall again. The only party that is filling the halls in this country—it’s called democracy, it’s called market share, and it’s called logic. Now come and learn; you just might find out something.
You see, the Greens have been here trying for Parliament since 1972; 54 years and they’ve never been in Cabinet—54 years, never been in Cabinet.

content.speaker: Francisco Hernandez
content.text: And we’re still bigger than you, mate. You won’t be around next time. Bye-bye, Winston! Bye-bye, Winston!

content.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
content.text: Oh, “Bye-bye, Winston!” Stand back, sunshine; I’ve got news for you. I’m coming back real big-time. We’re coming back with an army. We’re going to come back much bigger. Oh, don’t wave out to me. You should get up shortly and make your valedictory speech, because you guys are going to be out of here. No, we’re coming back—not for the first time. Out there, there are hundreds of thousands of people who’ve realised one thing: there’s a party that understands this country better than any other and that offers real hope for tomorrow. Thank you very much.

content.speaker: RAWIRI WAITITI (Co-Leader—Te Pāti Māori)
content.text: Thank you. How generous. Thank you for that applause. Ngā mihi nui ki a koe e te Pīka. This is the second time I’ve mihi-ed you today. I just want, again, to pass on these sentiments and thank you for the hard mahi, and also to all the staff here in Parliament for making the House work. This is my last speech I will give in the House under this Government, but like Arnold Schwarzenegger said, I’ll be back. This has been the most anti-Māori, anti-Tiriti, anti-taiao, anti-worker Government in a generation, and they have finally run out of numbers on the clock. On 7 November, we will issue their move-on orders from this House.

This is a Government that challenged our resilience, who we are forced to activate against, and although we couldn’t count on them, we have run their numbers. It took them two days to disestablish Te Aka Whai Ora. They removed 24 Māori wards from local councils across Aotearoa; that’s 24 tables that will no longer have an unapologetic Māori voice. A hundred thousand voters—that’s how many people will be disenfranchised because the Government’s parties are afraid of our voting power. A hundred and eighty thousand women—that’s how many hard-working wāhine had their pay equity claims cancelled under urgency so that this Government could give out handouts to landlords and corporations.

They removed section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act, and they have weakened Treaty obligations across education, pae ora, and the Resource Management Act. There are 19 more Treaty clauses that they will weaken or remove if we don’t vote this Government out. Four million dollars—that’s how much taxpayer money was wasted on the failed Treaty principles bill. Fifty days—that’s how long Te Pāti Māori MPs were suspended from this House for daring to challenge the most racist and ignorant bill of this century. This Government overturned at least three major court decisions; they entrenched the theft of our foreshore and seabed with the marine and coastal area amendment bill; they protected the biggest polluters in Aotearoa from litigation; and they legalised the killing of those, Chlöe, pesky kiwis. They have prioritised the erasure of our rights and privilege of our whenua—wow.

Over 112,000 people in Aotearoa don’t know where they’re sleeping tonight. One in seven tamariki is living in poverty. One in four tamariki Māori is living in poverty. Māori continue to die seven years earlier than non-Māori, and Māori unemployment has gone from 6.8 percent to 10.8 percent under this Government’s watch. These are the numbers under this Government, yet when Te Pāti Māori challenges the lived reality of te iwi Māori in this House, we are met by excuses and justifications centred in statistics of crime reduction and incarceration. A Government that measures the success of te iwi Māori in crime reduction is one content with keeping our people incarcerated. A Government that measures its wealth in the tax breaks afforded to the 2 percent is one content with keeping its country in a cost of living crisis. A Government that measures its “clean, green” New Zealand image in only tourism sales is one content on allowing mining and drilling and the further degradation of whenua Māori for profit. A Government that measures its unity in the regression of equitable policies is one that doesn’t understand Te Tiriti o Waitangi and has never read Matike Mai.

When Te Pāti Māori stands in this House, this Government calls statements performative. I would argue that should be said for the Government’s ability to create positive change for this country. The Prime Minister can reject the characterisation of our questions in the House, but we reject how this House characterises te iwi Māori. Despite everything this Government has subjected te iwi Māori to over this term, and the harmful rhetoric and narratives they have generated, I want to share the real stories, and stats, our people live in: 312,000 people are on the Māori roll; 100,000 people hikoi-ed  against the Treaty principles bill and this Government; 300,000 submitted against the Treaty principles bill; and te iwi Māori’s population is now almost one million.

content.speaker: RAWIRI WAITITI
content.text: I will go to the back page, Mr Speaker; 8 November will be an opportunity for New Zealand to see a brand new Government. If you want to see more Māori in Parliament, if you want to see a one-term Government, and to maintain an unapologetic Māori voice, the only way you can do that is candidate vote Te Pāti Māori. That is how we do that. This is the last stand that this Government will make. Come 7 November, you’ll be bye, bye, goodbye. Kia ora tatou.

content.speaker: Hon MARAMA DAVIDSON (Co-Leader—Green)
content.text: Democracy should work for all of us, not just the wealthy few. Te Tiriti has always been about taking the best possible care of each other, but right now a handful of very rich and powerful corporations can buy access and influence the Government for their private benefit.

In 2024, an Ipsos survey revealed that two-thirds of people feel that the economic system is rigged totally in favour of the rich and the powerful. Yet, it is Te Tiriti that has been weaponised as being divisive, despite the generosity that Māori have shown to all people for generations, whether it is marae opening up when the roads are closed, feeding and caring for multitudes of strangers with the utmost manaaki, whether it is iwi and hapū restoring the health of our rivers and oceans, native forests, and native taonga species for all of our mokopuna to enjoy, whether it is iwi and hapū providing social and health services to whoever needs it in their communities.

They label Te Tiriti as being divisive, despite the overwhelming majority of select committee submissions from the public and diverse organisations pleading to the Government that Te Tiriti and the relationships with local Māori have been vital to improving their work; that’s churches, unions, local and regional governments, local businesses, even developers, environmental groups, migrant groups, professional bodies, health bodies, and just ordinary members of the public who outright reject the attempts of these Government parties to sow division, who come with all the receipts of how Te Tiriti is one of the last bastions of protection for the environment, for workers, and for a community voice. That is why Te Tiriti is the target: because it stands in the way of the outright exploitation of our living systems, of workers’ rights and safety, and of community voice.

Which brings us back to where the real, unelected representation has always been, and it’s not Māori on boards wanting to ensure there is accountability for environmental protection that benefits everybody. No, the real unelected representation has always been the underhand, backdoor connections between political parties who are refusing to tax their billionaire and big corporate donors, and who instead want working people like tradies and nurses and the local barbers to keep paying twice the effective tax rate of someone who owns 50 houses. To copy and paste the demands of the wealthy straight into their law; that is where the real divide has always been.

The good news is that the Green Party will take big money out of politics. We will cap political donations at $30,000 and ensure that only people can donate and not companies. The Green Party has consistently stood by our values and our evidence-based policy solutions, to prioritise the wellbeing for the many and not just the few. We have not just a powerful opportunity to get rid of this Government, who have shown outright that they are here to serve billionaires, and bugger everyone else, but people have the chance to demand a Government that prioritises affordable living, healthy nature, and democracy for all of us, not just the powerful. Thank you.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLA WILLIS (Minister of Finance)
content.text: Well, I thought that was a very good example of the co-leadership in action. Marama Davidson has certainly been taking Chlöe Swarbrick’s advice to touch grass. I think the only problem is there is such thing as touching too much grass.

Colleagues, this is a time for gratitude, and I want to express some gratitude to a few people; first of all, to you, Mr Speaker: this is the first term of Parliament I have not been kicked out once, and I want to recognise you for that. Thank you.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Well, thank you for highlighting my failures.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLA WILLIS
content.text: Ha, ha! In particular, I want to acknowledge the extremely special piece of correspondence I received from you—in your handwriting—reminding me, as the Minister of Finance, of the existence of the Parliament Act 2025. I shall always treasure that correspondence.

I want to also acknowledge the staff at Copperfields, especially the baristas who pour long blacks directly into my veins, along with all of the unsung heroes of the precinct: the cleaners, the messengers, security guards, the Crown car drivers. These people don’t just deliver apricot danishes—but they do do that—they provide numerous moments of genuine kindness every day in this place. Chamber staff, Office of the Clerk, Parliamentary Counsel Office, Parliamentary Library, researchers—all these people who keep the democracy going. The members of the Press Gallery: in an age of declining trust, short-format video, clickbait, you soldier on and democracy is better for it, thank you.

I want to acknowledge my caucus colleagues in the National Party, and also our dedicated National Party members and volunteers all over the country. They are the very, very best people, and I am so looking forward to campaigning with them.

Our coalition colleagues: it has been an honour to have delivered this country’s first three-way coalition, and boy oh boy, have we got stuff done. Yes, there have been things on which we have differed, but we have gotten so much done for the good of this country.

I want to acknowledge the agency staff, especially, in my case, the Budget and fuel response teams; departmental private secretaries; my extraordinary political office staff, who have saved me from so many potential troubles, and whose grace and kindness continues to astound me.

But I feel that while we have achieved a lot for New Zealand—the first tax relief in 14 years; Investment Boost, ensuring tax incentives for those investing in growth and development; extending contributions to KiwiSaver; the tightest spending allowances in years, and yet prioritising investments in things that really matter: 33 new cancer drugs on our watch; the biggest boost for special education in our schools in decades; the FamilyBoost payment to help parents with the costs of early childhood education; funds in each of our Budgets to restore the dignity of the New Zealand Defence Force and the men and women who put their lives on the line for our country; backing our police; building infrastructure; getting things done.

But it is wrong in a speech like this to save all congratulations for the Government. I do want to recognise the Opposition. I really want to hand out some awards to them. I think the first thing we need to recognise is that if Parliament handed out medals for political gymnastics, Labour would have swept the podium this term. Yesterday, in a routine that would have scored a perfect 10 from the East German judge, Chris Hipkins performed the finest backflip this House has seen in a very long time. For three years, that member, backed up by his chorus of MPs, has practised one routine and one routine only. For every problem that has been ever described under this fair sun, he has had something to blame: it’s the tax cut for landlords! Interest deductibility—that was the problem. Whether it was the cost of living, whether it was unemployment, whatever it was, the problem was tax cuts for landlords. But then yesterday, we had a dismount, and we had—what I’ve been told they call in gymnastics—is a case of the “twisties”. Now, what happens with the twisties is that when you’re rotating in mid-air, you suddenly lose your sense of direction—completely lose your sense of direction—don’t know what’s up, what’s down, where you’re going, what you’re doing, and you panic. You panic in mid-air when you get the twisties, and I think this is what happened to Chris Hipkins yesterday. He was in mid-air, he realised he had no plan, he had no policies, he had no energy for the campaign, and he went, “Actually, I’m going to flip it and reverse it. That is exactly what he did.

Speaking of routines gone wrong: Ginny Andersen—can we just recognise her? She tried her signature move on live radio a few weeks ago, telling Mark Mitchell that road maintenance is not funded by the National Land Transport Fund. “You don’t even know what you’re talking about.”, she told him. “It’s a separate fund—you need to go check that.”—you need to go check that—“[if] you want to be credible on financial things, then you’re really kidding yourself.” She learned the truth during the ad break: there is no separate fund for road maintenance. She attempted a Hipkins-like backflip to correct herself, face planted on the mat, and then— this is the impressive part—got up and instead insisted that the beam had moved.

She is said to be receiving some coaching from Willie Jackson, her senior colleague, who is a master at never letting the facts, or your absence of policy, get in the way of the story. In fact, in Willie’s experience, the best way not to let the policy get in the way is to be blissfully unaware of it—that way, you don’t even have to defend it, you can just say, “I don’t know, ask Barb.”

This is actually someone I do want to spend some time on. On the one hand, I see in the member for Mana, a lack of imagination—51 times she’s asked me the same question this term. But on the other hand, I feel genuine sympathy for Barbara Edmonds, and let me let me tell you why: because she is surrounded by people who know one thing and one thing only, and that is how to spend other people’s money. That’s what they’ve done all their political careers, and that’s what they want to do with the rest of their political careers. They have gone out there and they’ve promised, so far, $18 billion worth of promises. And they’ve said, “Barb will tell you how she’s going to pay for it”. Barbara’s been sitting there with the calculator, trying to make it add up, and she knows it won’t add up. Maybe one of the little fig leaves she was holding on to with hope was, “Well, I think the leader will let me raid the landlords for the interest deductibility. I think I’ll do that.”—but, no, even that little glimmer of hope was taken away from her yesterday. But the good thing for Barbara is she knows that in a case of emergency, she can break glass. What is in that little glass that she can break if she really can’t make it add up? Well, the good news is Craig Renney’s got some ideas.

He’s been a bit painful for her, he’s been kind of competing for the role, but Chris Hipkins put him down the list, so he’s got his message. But he has come up with the idea—he said, “Look, this whole idea on a capital gains tax (CGT), don’t make it narrow, make it comprehensive.”, and that’s his plan. I just want to say with friends likeCarmel Sepuloni, Barbara—I don’t know how you do it. She was asked, on Morning Report, how Labour was going pay for its promises, and this is what she opened with: “Well, we certainly wouldn’t be giving tax breaks to landlords.” That was her answer! Poor Barbara, she’s left there going, “How on Earth do I make it up?”

But here’s the thing—actually look at the mates they’ve got in the Greens and Te Pāti Māori. Yes, Chris Hipkins is half baked and he’s got no energy and he’s got no policies, but look, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori are brimming with ideas, they’re generating new taxes every minute. And don’t worry: Chris Hipkins says. “Well, trust us, we’ve sort of ruled it out.” This is the same guy who said he’d never deliver a CGT—and what’s he campaigning on? A CGT. If the leader of the Opposition can backflip on tax deductibility in the space of one press conference, why should anyone believe a thing he rules out between now and polling day? You can’t trust Labour on tax. You can’t trust Hipkins. There is a way forward for this country, we stick to the plan—no new taxes. Don’t let Labour ruin it all again.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: The Hon—[Interruption] At least start with a bit of silence. I call The Hon Carmel Sepuloni.

content.speaker: Hon CARMEL SEPULONI (Deputy Leader—Labour)
content.text: In about 6½ weeks, the Hon Nicola Willis is going to look back on that speech and think, “Is that really the valedictory I wanted to deliver?”

I do want to reiterate some of the thanks to the staff that have been given by many of those that have spoken before me today. I also want to acknowledge you, Mr Speaker, even though Willie Jackson is speaking to you—not the first time that Willie Jackson has interrupted anyone—and, Mr Speaker, I want to acknowledge that I sit rather close to you and I do have a voice that carries—

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Yep.

content.speaker: Hon CARMEL SEPULONI
content.text: —so thank you for your tolerance over the course of this term.

I’m going to take a slightly different tack and acknowledge the fact that we are all going into campaign mode. Campaigns are hard work. They are not for the faint-hearted. I’m pretty seasoned now—not as seasoned as some in here—and as an experienced campaigner, I thought I’d offer up some do’s and don’ts to Government parties as we all head out into the wilderness of the campaign trail. These particular words of advice that I’m going to offer up are based mostly on the learnings of the past three years, observing the members of current Government parties, a Government that will go down in history as the coalition of chaos, and a Government that will be the first ever one-term National Government.

Now, what not to do on the campaign trail. My first piece of advice: do not ride scooters on the campaign trail. As we all know, our emergency departments do not have the capacity, let alone the nurses, to deal with avoidable injuries, particularly given there’s been only 54 additional nurses added over the last two years.

Second piece of advice: steer away from discussing sports teams when you know nothing about sport. No one wants to be the guy who refers to his childhood respect for the Crusaders when the Crusaders did not even exist during his childhood; and no one wants to be the guy that gets the Waratahs and the Warriors confused.

Do not say, “What I would say to you”. People can see and hear when someone is talking out loud. You are not thinking in your head. There is no need to premise every answer with that statement. Best not to talk about growth, growth, growth, Nicola Willis. When people hear National say those words three times in a row, they think they are referring to the growth in unemployment, the growth in business liquidations, and the growth in Kiwis moving overseas. Even if the three words were said by Nicola Willis whilst she was clicking her heels together, no one would end up in a better place.

Please, also—and this is a serious one—do not pretend to be political parties who support women. Women are not stupid. The scrapping of pay equity and the decision not to pay women what they are worth will go down in the books as one of the most shameful acts of this Luxon-led Government.

Now, on to the do’s for the campaign. It’s important for politicians to sound like they are in touch with the everyday experiences of New Zealanders. Telling them to cry you a river when talking about the cost of living is out of touch. Try hard, Government parties, to be honest about the alternative policy positions of other parties. People will tire of lies about taxes. I know how hard it must be for the current Government having nothing positive to talk about after three years, but people can sniff the desperation, and it is not mana-enhancing for any of you.

What parties must do is look like they actually support their boss. Two failed coups in National haven’t helped with their boss’s credibility. To be honest, you already look like the try-hard dad in the schoolyard or at the PTA meeting before his own team turned on him. I know that’s a little bit mean, but so was scrapping pay equity.

Most importantly, keep at the forefront of all statements and actions what is important to New Zealanders. Their jobs; not the jobs of politicians. Their health; not the healthy size of some political party donations. Their homes; not the multiple homes of those politicians trying to avoid a capital gains tax. Their cost of living; not the $60 a week one guy reckons is all he needs to do his grocery shopping. And finally, their country; the one thing they love, and the one thing they feel has gone backwards. It may hurt Government parties whilst out on the campaign trail when they hear people say over and over again that they simply cannot do three more years of this National-led Government. Suck it up and remember: “Better starts now”.

content.speaker: Hon WILLIE JACKSON (Labour)
content.text: Well, that’s the end of the most anti-Māori, anti-worker, anti-rainbow, anti-disability, anti - New Zealand Government that we have seen in our lifetime. You’ve got to ask yourself, why are they so weak? Well, because they’ve got a weak Prime Minister, who has allowed David Seymour and Winston Peters to take this country to a place that would shame Chris Finlayson, shame Jim Bolger, and shame Sir Douglas Graham.

The Prime Minister can’t control New Zealand First and ACT, and they have polled 6 percent and 8 percent. My God, imagine the nightmare—imagine the nightmare and the influence—if they return with greater majorities. We’ll fight to make sure this never happens.

content.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
content.text: Bye, bye, Willie. Haere rā, haere rā!

content.speaker: Hon WILLIE JACKSON
content.text: We’ll never forget what they’ve done—never forget what they’ve done. Their assault on Te Tiriti obligations. The Waitangi Tribunal found the Crown’s approach to the education changes breaches Treaty principles. That means nothing to Shane Jones. He’s a disgrace to his people in the North. He no longer supports principles he formerly supported when he was a young, recognised, and principled young man.

This racist friction that came about through the Treaty principles referendum cannot be complete without us acknowledging the honourable member for Epsom; the member who, this year, has managed the extraordinary feat of introducing a bill, losing it in the largest protest march in New Zealand history, and then telling us all he won. I mean, how delusional is that? The Treaty principles bill, 300,000 submissions against; the Regulatory Standards Bill opposed by every major Māori organisation, every legal academic who submitted, and at last count, the entire common-sense caucus of New Zealand; but the member for Epsom marches on, because he’s on a mission—a mission to erase kaupapa Māori and change the Treaty.

Meanwhile, on the National benches, the Prime Minister, whose biggest achievement this term was to fend off Chris Bishop and Erica Stanford and his mates—we want to thank the Prime Minister. We want to thank him very much for staying the Prime Minister. He’s Labour’s best chance of winning this election. He’s not here, but I wanted to thank him and acknowledge his acknowledgment of me earlier in the day.

content.speaker: Hon Mark Mitchell
content.text: And you’re our best chance of staying in Government.

content.speaker: Hon WILLIE JACKSON
content.text: You know this, Mark Mitchell; you’re in big trouble. When you look at the Public Service and what’s happened here, at a time when every second news story is about the Public Service failing in terms of underfunding, they attack the Public Service. Look at the economic vandalism that sees one in three Pacific kids in poverty, one in four Māori kids in poverty, 5.6 percent unemployment, 10.8 percent unemployment for Māori. And, of course, let’s not forget the fast-track development that weakened environmental protections—

content.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
content.text: Fast track! Gold! Gold!

content.speaker: Hon WILLIE JACKSON
content.text: —for Shane Jones’ donor mates. For Shane Jones—that’s what the Greens said—and for their mates. We’ll never forget the school lunches, where hungry kids became an experiment in how cheaply lunch could be made, thanks to Mr Seymour again. What about the appalling pay parity betrayal? New Zealand women must never forget the betrayal of this coalition Government. New Zealand women do not count for this Government. They are a disgrace. Pay parity means so much to us, and we will change the position and reinstate equity.

This Government came to office promising to fix the basics. Instead, they have made it worse. Three years later, unemployment rose, thousands of public servants went, hungry kids became the norm, environmental protections were weakened, and Māori spent the term watching rights and Treaty obligations stripped from statute after statute.

They told New Zealand they were cutting bureaucracy, then spent three years restructuring the machinery of government. They told us they were restoring accountability, while their own officials warned that some of the Treaty changes had no apparent benefit and risked serious damage in the Crown-Māori relationship.

Perhaps that arrogance, in terms of ignoring officials, is how we should remember this lot. Because when the experts warned them, they knew better. When communities protested, they knew better. When Māori marched, they knew better. Well, now there’s one group of New Zealanders whom they don’t get to tell that they know better, and that’s the voters. Kia ora Mr Speaker.

content.speaker: TĀKUTA FERRIS (Te Tai Tonga)
content.text: Mr Speaker, tēnā koe. [Authorised reo Māori text to be inserted by the Hansard Office.]
[Authorised translation to be inserted by the Hansard Office.]

Mr Speaker, thank you, and thank you for the call today. I’m going to take my opportunity to just present a little bit about what hope and vision has looked like for te iwi Māori over the last 50 years. The story of advancement and development for te iwi Māori over the last 50 years has been one of clear vision, of hope, of determination driven by the people. It’s never been about gaining things from Parliament and Governments, although they’ve played their role. The people have driven that growth and that development. We thank everyone involved, and to the people, [Authorised reo Māori text to be inserted by the Hansard Office.], and the people of Te Tai Tonga, tēnā koutou.

The debates, or the kōrero, this afternoon—it’s quite defensive, you know? It’s what we’ve done, and what we haven’t done, what they’ve done or what they haven’t done, what we’re going to do—all of this type of thing. But, really, the people in our country need to hear vision. They need to hear vision and commitment, drive, hope. What does the future Aotearoa look like, instead of just stones going across the aisle here?

And then I’m reminded of some things that great Māori leaders have said. One of them was Dr Ranginui Walker. And he said, “I have little time for people in privileged positions in our country, who use that privilege to attack the most vulnerable of our society.” Those aren’t my words; those are Dr Ranginui Walker’s words.

And as I think about the actions of this House over the last three, six, 30, 50 years, they ring true—they ring true. They are great words that last for ever, not like these ones that are just going to be here now and gone later. But those people shaped the course of Māori development. Those people shaped the course of Māori building out of what is one of the darkest ages for any people across the globe. And the story of Māori advancement, Māori development, is one of those stories. Māori have to live with the reality of it. The Māori whānau out there, living right throughout Aotearoa, have to live in the reality of it, and the reality is crippling.

Our people were once trapped in low-income work and poverty-type situations. They’re now firmly entrenched in poverty and homelessness. They are being shuffled further and further down the ranks, slipping through the cracks, while some in the country just keep going the other way. But when the majority are left behind and a few advance, that’s not the story of a people’s development; that’s the story of the development of only a few. And it ultimately won’t last.
Our development and our potential as a people has always been in our hands, e te whānau. It’s always been in our hands, and our story of Māori advancement, Māori development, is an astonishing one.

Over the last 50 years we’ve reclaimed more ground than was taken from us in 180 years, and that frightens a lot of people. The parliaments and people of power and influence in this country held that power in their hands for a very, very long time, and in the last 30, 40, 50 years, that grip has slowly come undone. And that’s an uncomfortable thing, for them. But what we should never forget is that that’s the story, that’s the reality, and despite the temperament of Governments that come and go, we remain and the story of advancement continues.

The Māori economy is one of the newest players, the newest pieces, in that development story, and everyone is all of a sudden interested in it. I’m reminded of the words of Whata Winiata, who said to us as a people that the best way for us to reclaim and retain our rangatiratanga and our mana motuhake is to behave as if we never lost it. And the story of Māori development is that in action, e te iwi, so make sure that we keep that in our hearts—those things that our rangatira said over decades, and has been the bedrock, the driving engine of the vision, the hope, the determination of te iwi Māori, and that is how we continue on. [Authorised reo Māori text to be inserted by the Hansard Office.]
[Authorised translation to be inserted by the Hansard Office.]

content.speaker: MARIAMENO KAPA-KINGI (Te Tai Tokerau)
content.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. This is a first, again, for me, to provide an adjournment speech. I’ve listened to a few so far, and I’m thinking, “Shucks, is that how those things are meant to go?” So I’m thinking, well, no, that’s not, from my point of view. So I’m going to approach it in a different way.

Firstly, the obvious thing to say is to thank you, Mr Speaker, for looking after us in this particular piece of this Whare—and I think in a good way, and I think in a fair way, and a loving way. So mihi atu ana ki a koe.

And I acknowledge the other Speakers as well, who in fact I had the opportunity to travel to Japan with, at your request. Thank you for that, too, because it was a bit of a homecoming for me, having the time that I spent there, and I appreciated being back in that particular piece of the world.

Ironically, you might recall, Mr Speaker, that we were at a summit meeting, which is interesting because it’s important in this context, because you never know when your name and your children’s names are going to show up. Suddenly somebody on this summit table on that side asked me about my son’s name, because he meets him every three months in Nelson. So, again, you know, it’s interesting, the privilege and the responsibility that this role provides us, which I’m grateful for, by the way.
To all the clerks and all the coffee makers, and all the people that keep this House warm, and look after us, mihi atu ana ki a koutou katoa.

I want to mihi to my mate Doc, sitting right here. I want to mihi to him—he’s a great man, he’s a loving man, he’s a family man, he’s a fisherman, and he backed me. And he backed me in one of the most important times that I needed that. He backed me—

content.speaker: Tom Rutherford
content.text: An absent man from the House.

content.speaker: MARIAMENO KAPA-KINGI
content.text: Tom, that’s enough, thank you, or whoever else is chatting over there. He backed me, as good men do, and I’m grateful for that, because that’s why I get the opportunity to remain in this House for Te Tai Tokerau and bring this speech to you today.

I want to acknowledge the team. So we’ve got Tapi and Sue and Maia. I want to say Maia’s name because Maia is beside me all the time doing the work that I need to be able to do to stand and take these speeches, and present at select committee. So, Maia, to you, big love to you, darling; good for you for sticking with me.

In my maiden speech, I referred to the word “lioness”, because everyone, when they knew I was coming here, just said, “Gee, Meno, you’re going down to that lion’s den.” You might recall I said, “That’s true, except it’s the lionesses that do the hunting, and get the work done.” So, as a lioness, yeah, again the importance of being able to be in this House for Te Tai Tokerau and—and I expect to do that on 8 November when I have my job interview on 7 November; I expect to come back and continue to do that.

But I also have a lion cub; as all good lionesses do, you have lion cubs, and I have a lion cub. He happened to be the one that led the biggest march in this country to the steps out here, and his name is Eru Kapa-Kingi. And he’s obviously known for other bits and pieces in this House, but, most importantly, he led the march from Te Rerenga, where I was born, all the way here, with near to 100,000 people, based on love, compassion, and for all people. He knew then what our tupuna Parāone Ngāruhe signed in 1840, and I’ve trained my kids to know this: that you must stand, you must fight, and you must speak for your people—Te Tai Tokerau people, Māori people, and all people that share this land. I want to make sure to make that mentioned in this adjournment speech.

Then, in closing, I just want to say this: I went to this interesting meeting the other night—it was a “meet the candidates”. You wouldn’t necessarily find me there, because there are lots of farmers and foresters and food producers, but it was one of the best meetings, because I once was a farmer, right? In fact, just before I came here, I used to manage 3,000 bulls, 37 ropes of mussels up in Te Kao, and I learnt what a R1 was and an R2 and what bull collars are and what fences are, and how much grass seed I need to make that cow fat to get it to McDonald’s. So, yes, I do know something about Māori economic development, and I want to be part of that after 7 November.
It has been a pleasure, even when it’s been a pain, to sit amongst you, to debate with you, and have a “pint of order” with you. Kia ora tātou.

content.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN (Minister of Health)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Well, it’s the last day of Parliament in this term, and for some of the people across the other side of the House, you can see they are a little bit exhausted getting all the way to the finish line. For some of them, they might even need a little bit of rest, a little bit of sleep, in order to get there.

Of course, Chris Hipkins, with that lacklustre speech he gave at the start, you could tell why he made his slogan “Better start now”: because it’s not just about helping him warm up; it’s like a self-motivational statement. Every time he’s driving around the country, he says, “Better start now.” Well, the reality is he doesn’t actually drive around the country, as the Prime Minister says. He only manages to get as far as Rongotai, to the south, and slightly north of the Remutakas, to those public meetings. Well, of course, we wish him well as he tries to warm up for the campaign and get started.

For some people, when they’re sleeping, they like to count sheep, don’t they? Some like to count sheep. Well, some in this House also like to count nurses, as I’ve been hearing, quite obsessively. As tradition is in these adjournment debate speeches, having some numbers is always a helpful thing. Well, for the last time in this Chamber this term, there are 1,640 additional fulltime-equivalent nurses under this Government—a huge achievement. I’d encourage members who are trying to “better start now”, or just warm up, that counting to 1,640 might aid them with their sleep; it might put them to sleep.

Here are some other numbers: one—that’s the number of cats at Chris Hipkins’ first public meeting. No one knows what the cat said, only that the cat attended, but no one knows exactly what anyone else said, either. In fact, I have four children and we sometimes have more people at our home for dinner than attend a public meeting with the Labour Party. The number four—that’s how many parties will be needed for the left and the far left to be able to form a coalition Government after the next election: Labour, Greens, Te Pāti Māori, and Opportunity. What a disaster this country is going to avoid on 7 November. Of course, two of the four parties each have co-leaders, so that’s six leaders of one potential Government. What that adds up to—you know, maths and all of that. I must acknowledge Erica Stanford. She’s doing a great job getting our kids reading and writing. That all adds up to one big shambles, because 10 percent of the combined caucuses would be leaders.

The four parties, with their six co-leaders, are all promoting nine new taxes between them—nine new taxes between them. Well, at least nine new taxes, because they’ve got the capital gains tax from the Labour Party, but we’re not sure if that’s a capital gains tax or, as Craig Renney says, maybe it’s a “comprehensive capital gains tax”—ask Barb—a 45 percent top tax rate, an asset tax, an inheritance tax, a digital tax, a gift tax, a business tax, a rental tax, and a land tax. In fact, if you look at all their taxes, they will tax you on your income while you’re living; they’ll tax your house if you’ve got a rental property; and they’ll tax you on your inheritance when you die. In fact, they’ll keep taxing you—a land tax, which will be on top of your rates, as well. I know there’s also a proposition for a death tax, which means they’ll keep taxing you after you die. That’s the reality of the Labour Party, the Green Party, the Opportunity Party, and Te Pāti Māori. They want to tax, tax, tax, and this election is going to be about tax.

Some of our achievements: here are some more numbers: “32”—a 32-year high. That was inflation under the previous Government. They did it once, and the reality is they could do it again. That’s not a challenge—that’s not a challenge—even though I have no doubt they could rise to it, because that’s exactly what they’d do: spend more, tax more, borrow more. That’s why we’re campaigning so hard against the taxes at this year’s election. Eighteen billion dollars—that is the gap between what a Labour Government wants to spend and the money they’ve got available from just their taxes, just their taxes. That’s not the Greens’, Te Pāti Māori’s, and Opportunities’ taxes. No wonder they need those taxes from the other parties, because they’ve got no way of actually being able to deliver it themselves. The last number is unknown: the amount that Te Pāti Māori MPs have spent on lawyers; not to fight the system, just to fight each other. No one quite knows, do they?

Well, here’s some numbers on our side: zero. No new taxes under the next National Government. One oil and gas ban overturned this term. In three years, we’ve doubled the renewable generation that was commissioned—more in the last three years than in the previous eight. Five health targets, and all of them improved under this Government; they declined under the previous Government. Fourteen years: that’s how long New Zealanders waited for tax relief until this Government came to office and delivered it. Sixty-six new medicines, including 33 new cancer medicines, making a huge difference for patients up and down our country. Four percent: the new rates cap that we’re putting in place, which Labour still doesn’t know what they think about. Nine hundred and forty additional doctors, and add to that the 1,640 nurses you count at night if you’re an insomniac. We also have 14,200 fewer New Zealanders on the elective treatment waiting lists waiting over more than four months.

There is so much that’s been achieved and so much more to do, but of course, every election is a choice. I want to just highlight the choice and the member of the Opposition, the Opposition leader. I call him the Opposite of the Midas man—you know, the opposite of Midas. I’ve got four young children, and I love reading them stories. One of their favourites is, of course, the story of King Midas, who turns around and touches everything and it turns to gold. Well, the Leader of the Opposition, the man who wants to be Prime Minister, he’s got the opposite of the Midas touch. He was Minister of Education and achievement kept sliding; Minister of Police and ram raids became a nearly daily event under his watch, while gangs flaunted their regalia on our streets. Minister of Health: wait-lists and emergency department waits blew out. Minister for the Public Service: 47,000 public servants became 65,000 public servants, growing three times faster than the workforce at large.

Minister for COVID-19 Response: well, he forgot to order the vaccine, and kept Auckland locked down longer than needed. Of course, he then didn’t even follow the health advice, as the royal commission has now confirmed. Chris Hipkins doesn’t have a record of fixing things. He has a record of breaking things; in fact, breaking everything he touches. He’s failed upwards, and now he wants the top job again. So, when Chris Hipkins asks New Zealanders to trust him and this country again, understand what you’re actually being asked; not to trust someone new but to trust the man who’s already run the Police, the Public Service, Health, Education, and the Covid-19 response, and delivered exactly what you just heard.

In closing, it’s important that we thank all of the people who play such an important role here at this House. We want to thank you, Mr Speaker, Deputy Speaker, and Assistants. I do try hard to be good, as you know, Mr Speaker. The officials who have worn the carpet, coming in and out of my office, from Energy, Health, State Enterprises, Transport, Auckland, that I’ve held over this term; my private secretaries; my political office staff, electorate office staff, electorate team.

It’s also important to acknowledge the families. In this Chamber, all of us know the price of us doing this job. To my own family, especially my wife Rebecca, my four children, for whom, too often, I’m simply a face on screen saying goodnight at bedtime—thank you very much.

Finally, my favourite number: it’s 45 days until the election, when New Zealanders choose who they trust to form the next Government. I say to the Opposition: don’t take it personally, but I hope to see fewer of you when we return to the House. I also wish everyone all the very best on the campaign trail. Good luck and may the team offering the fewest taxes win.

content.speaker: GLEN BENNETT (Labour)
content.text: Fifty-four is the magic number, not of today, but of the whole of the term. He talked about the favourite number that he has, in the countdown to the election, but Mr Simeon Brown is the “54 nurses” man. I think, if we look back, we have Studio 54, which was a famous studio that was famous for glamour and glitz and parties and celebrities—very opposite to the current National Party; they have none of that. As I listened in, the comment was made about being continually obsessed with the Labour Party; all they could talk about was us—in fact, for the last three years. All I can say is, if they’re still talking about fixing the basics, it’s because, clearly, the basics are pretty broken for themselves and what they’ve done, and they need to obsess more on what they’re going to do, as opposed to what we are going to do.

Now, three years is a long time in this place. For me, it was a different experience. At the start of this term, I was out, then I was back in—something you won’t often hear a gay man say, but I will say that this afternoon. For many of you in this room, this will be your last time in this space. We acknowledge the work that people have done and how tough that is, but I want to comment as the chief whip of the Labour Party and the privilege I’ve had, and the responsibility, to take on that role. I had one key performance indicator when I came into this role and that was to never be seen on the black and white tiles as a chief whip. You know what happens if a chief whip is standing on the black and white tiles? You have not done your job, because you’re standing behind an MP who’s either apologising or resigning. Thank the Lord—touch wood; we’ve got about 40 minutes left—it has not happened under my “whipship”. Thank you to my caucus for being so diligent, so focused, so passionate, and so driven; to my colleagues, to Tracey and to Cushla for your support. Also, I do acknowledge whips from across the aisle and the work that you do together.

I was listening really carefully as we gave our speeches and comments this afternoon, and David Seymour had some really interesting comments—which I would never have thought I’d bring up. He talked about this cultist church that he was drawing the Prime Minister into—his strange Seymour-ACT church. Well, if his church is one that is callous, if his church is one that punches down and is compassionless and is mean, that’s a pretty stink church, and I don’t want to be part of that church. I don’t think the Prime Minister should either. But then, if I look at the meanness and the punching down that we have seen this term—look at our trans whānau, our rainbow communities, our Māori, our ethnic communities, when it comes to working women, when it comes to 18- and 19-year-olds, our disability sector, the homeless, the list goes on and on and on—that is a church of unkindness and meanness and we will have no part of that.

As I was listening to the Rt Hon Chris Hipkins, as we’ve been preparing for the election over recent weeks and months, it’s really got me thinking about what church I want to be a part of. I think about Michael Joseph Savage. He talked about applied Christianity when it comes to the work of this place and looking after society. Then I look at the Rt Hon Dame Jacinda Ardern, and she talked about kindness, which, again, is that same thing, around how we look out for and work for people here in Aotearoa. And then, as I’ve listened to  Chris Hipkins, over recent months, he uses this phrase about “a fair go for everyone”—a fair go for everyone. I think that is what the people outside of this building are looking for: a fair go for everybody; lifting people up, not punching people down, being kind, not callous and rude. I want to be part of the Labour Party whānau and church that is advocating, that is lifting people up and not pushing people down.

We do want to say thank you, because we don’t always look this beautiful and sound as wonderful on our own. We do have people all over this building and around the country looking after us—when it comes to, I think, it’s Colin and Keith in the booth up there, keeping our microphones going; when it comes to our security teams; when it comes to our electoral office staff, our staff here in this building; when it comes to the caterers, the building team, the press gallery; when it comes to the library and Hansard; the cleaners, the clerks, the messengers, the Chamber staff, and, of course, you, Mr Speaker, for really holding this place together and in good stead.
We look forward to counting down to the election, and we look forward to having more nurses in our hospitals. Better starts now.
