content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON (Leader of the House)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I think, for anyone who is watching, they can tell it is the last day of school. It is the last day of the 54th Parliament. As the member of Parliament for Taupō—the very proud member of Parliament for Taupō—I do want to just reflect on this period of time. Every single one of the 123 members of Parliament who have sat in this House serve a number of people in their communities, and they do it with the best intent. But, today, primarily I rise as the Leader of the House, and I want to acknowledge our Prime Minister, the Rt Hon Christopher Luxon, and the privilege that he gave me in serving in this role. I want to acknowledge the support of my predecessor, the Hon Chris Bishop. We’ve worked together very closely over this term.

Most people look at this House, they look at this Chamber, as an amphitheatre of war, where members go into battle each and every day, and it’s something to win, something to endure—blood, sweat, and tears lie on the floor. It’s all about the legislative outcomes that people are willing to fight for, and that’s the end result, the political fight, the war which captures the media headlines. What is often not reported is the amount of work that goes in to getting a bill before this Parliament. I want to just run through some of the stats of the 54th Parliament, the collective efforts of the National Party, New Zealand First, and ACT: 230 pieces of legislation—210 Government bills, 14 members’ bills, four private bills, two local bills; 240 bills have been introduced by our Government this term. Yes, sometimes it’s felt like a bit of a political marathon. My thanks to this side of the House, who have endured many hours of urgency, overtime, over time. I do have to say the Hon Paul Goldsmith takes the gold medal for the most legislation, with 34 bills enacted. Chris Bishop comes up second, with 23. I’m a little bit down the medal table, on only 10. I do want to acknowledge the amount of effort that goes into each and every one of those bills—hundreds and hundreds of hours to get those pieces of legislation ready.

I want to acknowledge some of the unsung heroes in the parliamentary process. Firstly, we are blessed in this country with phenomenal public servants. They work incredibly hard to deliver for the Government of the day policy solutions to the problems that our communities and our countries face. Then there is the Parliamentary Counsel Office, more commonly known as PCO. They do incredibly hard yards, translating the policy ideas into legislation, and they often, in our term of Parliament, have had tight time frames to do that. I do want to acknowledge and shout out Cassie Nicholson KC, who is the Chief Parliamentary Counsel, and Richard Wallace, the Deputy Chief Parliamentary Counsel, who have been incredibly helpful for our Parliament and our Government, working through an enormous amount of legislation. There’s also the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet. There is also the legislation coordinator in the Cabinet Office and all of the staff who support the legislative process for our Cabinet committees. Of course, then, when it comes here, it is the Clerk’s team who are really significant in terms of making sure everything is correct according to the Standing Orders. There are also other teams that make sure the Parliament runs as best as it can. As well as the Clerk’s Office, there is the select committee staff, and Hansard.

I also want to draw on my own experiences of the 54th Parliament and reflect on the people in my own team who have helped progress those 10 pieces of legislation. In our team, we call it the “middle office”. Thank you to you all. I also want to thank somebody whose name is probably on more emails that run around this Parliament than anybody else. Of course, he would never have put his own name in a speech, but I do want to acknowledge my trusted House adviser Carlos Webster, who makes sure, with lots of challenges at times, that the legislation gets through the House on time. Also, as in every Minister’s office—and in our office, we call it the “Team Upston Class of 54”—there is an enormous team of private secretaries who are seconded from agencies. Every Minister has them. They are absolutely worth their weight in gold. I think the private secretaries who work in the Beehive are a particular special breed of public servants who deserve our acknowledgment today.

As I approach the end of my speech, I also want, given it’s the end of the 54th Parliament, to offer a shout-out to the Opposition members. We do know that, in terms of accountability, question time is a really important part of this process. The public must have confidence that Ministers will be questioned robustly and—Mr Speaker and your presiding officers—if they transgress, they will be held to account. I’m reliably informed that, during the 54th Parliament, I have faced 153 primary questions, with only 99 of them coming from the other side. It is a really important part of the process.

As I said, 240 bills have been introduced by this Government, and they have all been about making New Zealand a better place for all New Zealanders. One group of people that we could not do without are the incredible staff who work in our electorate offices. To my electorate office team and to the electorate office teams of every member of Parliament, thank you for what you do.

I want to just have a look at the legislation that our Government has passed, because we have been fixing the basics; lowering inflation and interest rates to begin easing the cost of living; reducing taxes on Kiwis so they keep more of their own money; making it easier for Kiwis to farm, to build, and to grow businesses. National has continued to restore law and order, making New Zealand safer and putting victims at the heart of our justice system. We have been getting our kids back to school, teaching the basics and setting them up for life. And, of course, now, what are we doing? We are building the future. We are growing the economy to create more jobs and better opportunities for New Zealanders. We are maintaining disciplined spending so taxes are spent wisely. We’re upgrading roads, schools, hospitals, and giving Kiwis quality and reliable public services. By securing affordable housing for families and first-home buyers, hard-working Kiwis will have the security of owning their own home.

Do you know what, Mr Speaker? I thank you, and I thank your presiding officers, but I want to particularly thank the National Party team. You’re an extraordinary group of New Zealanders. I know how hard you work. I know how dedicated you are to serving our communities and our country, and I feel enormously proud to be part of team National. And guess what! We’ll be back after 8 November. We’ll be here to do it all over again for the 55th Parliament. There are two things to remember: firstly, under National, there will be no new taxes; and if that’s what you want, you’ve got one choice before the 7 November, and that is party vote National.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: It’s usual, at the conclusion of this debate, for the Speaker to offer not only some thanks but also some statistics to the House, but Louise, you’ve just completely stolen my thunder, which leaves me—

content.speaker: Hon Member
content.text: Kick her out!

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: I’m sure she’d be pleased to go, but it leaves me with some stats that aren’t quite so exciting, like Copperfields having sold 166,000 cups of coffee; 18,000 scones—Bish, where’s he; 5,690 doughnuts—that’s you, Willie, I think, is it? Oh no, it’s the pies, Willie—12,000 pies. Are you putting your hand up, Duncan?

content.speaker: Hon Dr Duncan Webb
content.text: Could be me.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Yeah, it could be. Most of all, I was asked if I would say that the brilliant catering manager, Mr Bryce Hughes, has a personal favourite, which is the 1,000 servings of mince on toast.

I want to put on the record an acknowledgment of all the work that all the members of this House have done over the past three years. It’s not an easy job and, as many have mentioned in their speeches, it does affect families and it does take people away from all of the normal things that people might do in life, and you do that because you have that commitment to the democratic process.

Inside of that, there’s always this talk about the hours that we work here. There’s a lot of people today mentioning urgency, etc. Breaking it down, this House does about 600 hours—or, over the last three years, about 615 hours a year. It may not seem a lot if people hear that in a bald sort of way, but the time that MPs put into all of the knowledge that they bring into this House, all of the views they bring to this House, and all of the ideas they bring to this House is extraordinary, and I don’t think we should allow people to get too fixated on the time that people spend here in the House. There are always people away doing stuff. What I’ve learnt as Speaker, working with the whips, who I really do have a lot of respect for, is that there is an enormous number of things that people do that require them to be away from this House, and I fully respect that.

I just want to add my thanks to the Clerk’s Office for the work that they do, not only with select committees but also here in the Chamber, and the Chamber staff as well. I want to thank the Chief Executive’s Office for the work they do in making everything that is Parliamentary Service work for members, and I want to thank the security staff for the work that they are doing. Security is one thing that we’ve had to improve significantly over the last three years, and the staff here have picked up on that extremely well, with a great deal of pride, and they now also work, of course, outside of Parliament should any of us need them.
I want to mention the catering staff. They do a great job. I mentioned them before. I also want to—

content.speaker: Hon Members
content.text: Ha, ha!

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Well, look, imagine what it’d be like spending your time making 5,000 doughnuts. You’ve got to respect that. I also want to thank my executive assistant Laree Taula, and I also want to thank Kellie for stepping in when Roland Todd retired. I also want to thank Alyson Groves, from Parliamentary Service, who has done 42 years here and is about to retire, as well. I should thank the triumvirate of advice that I’ve had over the last three years, and part of that triumvirate is Dr David Wilson, who’s our Clerk and is a very learned man, and I’ve enjoyed our discussions with him; and also Rafael Gonzalez-Montero, the Chief Executive of Parliamentary Service, who genuinely has the best interests of members at heart; and also, the person that makes them both good, Andie Lindsay, in the joint office, who I’m sure everyone knows.

I want to thank the VIP drivers—I’m just going through my list here—and I also need to thank Barbara Kuriger, Greg O’Connor, Teanau Tuiono, and Maureen Pugh for the work that they have done, sitting in here for those long hours of committee.

With those remarks, can I wish everyone well as we go out on to the campaign trail, allowing New Zealanders to make a choice about how they want to be governed, in one of the freest democracies in the world.
Motion agreed to.
The House adjourned at 5.55 p.m.

fullContent:
Wednesday, 23 September 2026
      The Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.

Start of Sitting Day
      Karakia/PrayersTEANAU TUIONO (Assistant Speaker) (14:00): E te Atua kaha rawa, ka tuku whakamoemiti atu mātou, mō ngā karakia kua waihotia mai ki runga i a mātou. Ka waiho i ō mātou pānga whaiaro katoa ki te taha. Ka mihi mātou ki te Kīngi, me te inoi atu mō te ārahitanga i roto i ō mātou whakaaroarohanga, kia mōhio ai, kia whakaiti ai tā mātou whakahaere i ngā take o te Whare nei, mō te oranga, te maungārongo, me te aroha o Aotearoa. Āmene.
      [Almighty God, we give thanks for the blessings which have been bestowed on us. Laying aside all personal interests, we acknowledge the King and pray for guidance in our deliberations that we may conduct the affairs of this House with wisdom and humility, for the welfare, peace, and compassion of New Zealand. Amen.]

Speaker's Statements
      Steve Streefkerk—Serjeant-at-Arms
      SPEAKER: Members, I’d like to notify the House that today marks the last sitting day that Steve Streefkerk, the Serjeant-at-Arms, will bear the mace. Steve has served in this role since 2016, after a distinguished naval career, including being Commander of HMNZS Te Kaha. We thank him for his dedicated service and wish him well for his next role.
      [Applause]

Privilege
      Development of Framework for Recommendations for Punishing Members for Contempt
      Referral to Privileges Committee
      SPEAKER: Members, the Standing Orders Committee has presented its report on the Review of Standing Orders 2026. The report will be debated today. One of the committee’s recommendations is that a general question of privilege be referred regarding a framework for reaching recommendations for punishing members for contempt.
      Historically, it has been very rare for the Privileges Committee to recommend that a member be suspended from the service of the House. There are only two known examples prior to this term of Parliament: one was for one day and one was for three days. The suspension of members in this term for as long as three weeks therefore represents a change in the House’s practice.
      In its report, the Standing Orders Committee said it would be useful for a framework to be developed for how punishments for contempt may be determined in the future. Such a framework or set of expectations would support the Privileges Committee in reaching recommendations that are seen as proportionate and consistent.
      A framework could set out factors for the Privileges Committee to consider when recommending punishments. It could also indicate steps to ensure a robust and fair process. For the public to have confidence in the House’s disciplinary procedures, it is important to avoid perceptions that they may be arbitrary in their operation.
      Although I can refer a question of privilege without a recommendation to do so, I believe the Standing Orders Committee’s report provides useful context for why a referral should be made. Accordingly, I find that a general question of privilege arises and stands referred to the Privileges Committee. I expect that consideration to be undertaken and commenced when the committee reconvenes in the next Parliament.

Presentation
      Petitions
      SPEAKER: Two petitions have been delivered for the Clerk to present.
      CLERK (14:03): 
      Petition of Consumer NZ requesting that the House better separate electricity generation and retail, ensure power prices reflect underlying costs, increase investment in renewable energy, and establish a long-term, cross-party energy strategy
      petition of Waimauku Community Association Incorporated requesting that the House amend the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 to prohibit the approval of the Waimauku West development, and prohibit approval of other housing outside areas identified for future growth unless necessary public infrastructure is planned and funded.
      SPEAKER: Those petitions stand referred to the Petitions Committee.
      Papers
      SPEAKER: Ministers have delivered two papers.
      CLERK (14:04): 
      2025-26 annual report for the Ministry for Women
      Government response to the report of the Petitions Committee on the petition of James Bond.
      SPEAKER: Those papers are published under the authority of the House.
      Select Committee Reports
      SPEAKER: Eight select committee reports have been delivered for presentation.
      CLERK (14:04): 
      Report of the Finance and Expenditure Committee on the briefing on the response to the inquiry into banking competition
      report of the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee on the Military Decorations and Distinctive Badges (Modernisation) Amendment Bill
      reports of the Health Committee on the
      briefing on endometriosis and petition of Endo Warriors Aotearoa
      briefing on mesh injury registries, and the
      review briefing on the 2024-25 annual review of the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission
      report of the Petitions Committee on the Petition of Wendy Joy Baker
      report of the Privileges Committee on the question of privilege concerning the release of a draft report of the Governance and Administration Committee
      report of the Transport and Infrastructure Committee on the inquiry into Ports and the Maritime Sector.
      SPEAKER: The bill is set down for second reading. The inquiry, briefings, and report of the Privileges Committee are set down for consideration.

Bills
      Customs and Excise (Border Security) Amendment Bill
      Introduction
      SPEAKER: The Clerk’s been informed of the introduction of a bill.
      CLERK (14:05): Customs and Excise (Border Security) Amendment Bill, introduction.
      SPEAKER: That bill is set down for first reading. We come now to oral questions, the first in the name of—

Points of Order
      Ministers—Correction of StatementsRICARDO MENÉNDEZ MARCH (Musterer—Green) (14:05): Point of order. Thank you very much, Mr Speaker. I just want to raise a serious matter on Ministers taking the first available opportunity to correct inaccurate or potentially misleading statements. This is the last opportunity a Minister has to do so. On the 15th of this month, Minister Louise Upston, when asked whether she had sought advice on the impact on sick, injured, and disabled New Zealanders and whether they had been left into debt, homelessness, or hunger, answered yes. I posed the very same question in writing, and, today, just now, a couple of hours ago, she came back to me with the exact opposite answer, which was an emphatic no. I’m concerned that Ministers are not taking the opportunity to correct statements when a week ago I got an emphatic yes to a question and in writing got a very clear no to the very same question.
      SPEAKER: Yeah, look, it’s fairly straightforward. I think the procedure for such contested responses like that is to either write to the Speaker or set down a notice of motion on the Order Paper. I appreciate that we are at the end of this Parliament, but, none the less, the Standing Orders remain in place.

Oral Questions to Ministers
      Finance
      Question No. 1RYAN HAMILTON (National—Hamilton East) (14:06) to the Minister of Finance: What has been the Government’s approach to tax in this parliamentary term?Hon NICOLA WILLIS (Minister of Finance) (14:06): Well, one of the proud achievements of this Government has been to deliver real tax relief to working people for the first time in 14 years, against the cries of Opposition. The Government inherited rapidly rising debt, persistent deficits, and high levels of spending. Our main priority has been to get the books back in order. We’ve been very disciplined with Government spending so that our fiscal repair job has not required new taxes, but it’s more than that. While getting the books back in order, we’ve also made significant tax changes that let people keep more of their own money, increasing support for working families and giving businesses an incentive to invest in productive assets that will grow the economy.
      Ryan Hamilton: What personal tax policies has the Government introduced?
      Hon NICOLA WILLIS: In 2024, the Government increased personal income tax thresholds and expanded eligibility for the independent earner tax credit. The effect of these changes was to deliver the first personal income tax relief for 14 years, and that tax relief went to working people. The Government also increased support for low to middle income working families, who got up to an extra $50 a fortnight, and we introduced FamilyBoost to help families with young children meet the costs of early childhood education. This was achieved within an overall operating package of $3.2 billion, which was significantly lower than recent Budgets under the previous Government. We managed to do a lot more for Kiwis’ back pockets through tax relief than the previous Government ever did.
      Ryan Hamilton: What business tax policies has the Government introduced?
      Hon NICOLA WILLIS: Well, the Government restored interest deductibility for residential rental property, returning to the normal practice of taxing profit, not revenue. While there were doubters, they have latterly had a road to Damascus experience on this one and recognised the value of this policy. In 2025, the Government introduced Investment Boost to encourage New Zealand businesses to make productive investments. It allows firms to immediately deduct 20 percent of the cost of a new asset, and this, of course, is an incentive to invest in machinery, tools, farm equipment, vehicles, industrial buildings, and other productive assets. Officials advised that this would increase productivity and lead to higher wages and higher employment, and, boy oh boy, the feedback from those who have used it is strong and positive.
      Ryan Hamilton: What is the alternative to this approach?
      Hon NICOLA WILLIS: Right now, people are very seriously proposing a capital gains tax. In fact, the Council of Trade Unions (CTU) in particular are promoting a comprehensive capital gains tax. I note that there are members of the CTU who are also prominently running in election seats this election.       Question No. 4Dr HAMISH CAMPBELL (National—Ilam) (14:25) to the Minister responsible for RMA Reform: What recent milestones have been achieved in the Government’s work to replace the Resource Management Act 1991?Hon CHRIS BISHOP (Minister responsible for RMA Reform) (14:25): As of around 9.45 p.m. last night, the Resource Management Act (RMA) has been repealed. After 35 years of the RMA being a millstone around the neck of this country, we’ve now passed legislation for a fundamentally different way of planning for New Zealand’s future, as I think there is widespread consensus in the Parliament that the RMA has made it slower, harder, and more expensive to build homes, infrastructure, grow the food, and build the energy we rely on. It’s failed to prevent environmental degradation; we’ve had the worst of both worlds. We now have a new system—narrower, simpler, faster, more consistent, more upfront about the trade-offs we need to make, to make sure that as a country we can grow and thrive.
      Dr Hamish Campbell: What are the key changes that have been made as part of these reforms?
      Hon CHRIS BISHOP: Unlike the RMA, most of the big decisions we made more upfront in the legislation and upfront in the system. It means we can stop relitigating the same questions over and over again through individual consent applications. One hundred planning documents will be replaced by 17 regional combined plans; we’ll have nationally standardised zones and rules to reduce variation across the country. Officials estimate around 45 percent of consent and permit applications currently required under the RMA could be removed under the new system. The economic benefits of these reforms are significant. Independent analysis projects the new planning system will boost GDP by an additional 0.56 percent every year by 2050, worth up to $3.1 billion annually. These are fundamentally good reforms to supercharge our economy.
      Dr Hamish Campbell: How important is the implementation of the new planning system going to be to its success?
      Hon CHRIS BISHOP: Passing the legislation is a significant achievement for the Government, but the hard work is just beginning. When Parliament passed the RMA in 1991, it was assumed that there would be a whole lot of extra work done after that, which never happened, so the Government is very focused on the implementation around spatial planning, around national direction, and around national standards over the next two to three years. We’re also focused on driving a culture change in the new system. The RMA encouraged a culture focused on process, repeated litigation, development treated as something to be constrained not enabled. We’re working hard at changing the incentives and we’re investing in implementation. Budget 2026 invested $294 million over four years to support the roll-out of our new planning system; more will be required but we are getting on with the job.
      Dr Hamish Campbell: What do the Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill do for New Zealand’s future?
      Hon CHRIS BISHOP: One of the things that I have been reflecting on over the last three years is that we are not as wealthy as a country as sometimes we think we are, and we are certainly nowhere near as prosperous as we should be. We are, indeed, at a crossroads. We can accept a low-growth past, present, and future; we can continue to be a relatively poor country, and the continued degradation of our natural environment, or we can take tough choices and make hard decisions. If we get it right, it means our children can access higher living standards, better education, better healthcare systems, and protect the natural environment. The RMA reforms that this Government has implemented represent tough decisions in the national interest to set New Zealand up for success in the 2030s. They are part of this Government’s plan to build the future.

      Question No. 6TODD STEPHENSON (ACT) (14:35) to the Minister for Regulation: What actions has the Government taken to reduce regulation for New Zealanders?Hon DAVID SEYMOUR (Minister for Regulation) (14:35): Thank you, Mr Speaker, and in keeping with other party leaders, I’d like to thank you for your grace and forbearance in trying to manage this place over the last three years. The establishment of the Ministry for Regulation and the Regulatory Standards Act are some of the institutions that we’ve created, and they have saved hundreds of millions of dollars already. However, the changes that the House voted through last night to replace the Resource Management Act with two new laws based on property rights—that will halve the number of consents required for the same amount of activity; that will add half a percent or about $3 billion a year to GDP—that is the largest, most significant change that this Government has made, and yet it is far from the only one in this Government of deregulation.
      Todd Stephenson: What has the Government done to reduce unnecessary regulation in health?

Standing Orders
      Adoption of AmendmentsHon LOUISE UPSTON (Leader of the House) (15:12): In accordance with the determination of the Business Committee, I move, That the House adopt the amendments to the Standing Orders set out in Appendix A of the report of the Standing Orders Committee on the Review of Standing Orders 2026, with effect from the day after the dissolution or expiration of the present Parliament.
      As we close out the 54th Parliament, we come to a debate held at the end of every term, one that I suspect only the deepest Parliament nerds will ever pay close attention to. Each term, the Standing Orders Committee needs to consider how Parliament operates and the rules it uses to keep things working well. It is an incredibly collaborative process, and I want to thank all of the members of Parliament who sat on the committee and worked through the changes before us. I also want to thank and acknowledge you, Mr Speaker, for presiding over the committee and ensuring the Standing Orders review was run in an efficient and considered way so that final decisions were not rushed. I also want to acknowledge the Clerk, Dr David Wilson, and his staff, particularly David Bagnall, for the tremendous amount of work that they have put into this report. 
      We discussed many issues during this process. I want to speak briefly about urgency, which was raised at length in submissions. I think a lot of people misunderstand urgency. A bill being included in an urgency motion does not in itself mean it is bypassing scrutiny or has been poorly drafted. In this Parliament, urgency has largely been used as overtime. Only 10 bills skipped select committee this term, outside the first 100-day plan and the normal Budget urgency. Part of the reason urgency has been used in that way is this is the first three-party coalition Government, which has placed additional pressure on legislative priorities. Bills have also, in general, taken significantly longer at the committee of the whole House stage than in previous Parliaments. I do want to note that the committee has agreed to changes that I think will encourage a better use of urgency, including requiring Ministers to explain why they need to bypass select committee, and I hope that will help demonstrate that when urgency is used, it is for good reason. 
      By far the biggest change we have agreed to is the establishment of the Legislative Scrutiny Committee which will act as a kind of second Chamber for the House. This committee will be able to take the place of the committee of the Whole House for non-controversial bills that would not normally receive high priority in any Government’s programme. The committee will be chaired by the Deputy Speaker and will not have a Government majority. The intention is that almost everything referred to it will be broadly supported, so that votes are rare. The Standing Orders Committee has thought carefully about how the legislative scrutiny would examine legislation and what would be referred to it, but thought experiments do not enact legislation, so it is important that we see that it is tested once the new Parliament begins.
      There were other changes agreed by the committee that should make Parliament a better place for the public to engage with. I personally am particularly pleased to see a change requiring MPs who are on the parliamentary precinct to attend select committee meetings in person during sitting weeks, rather than by joining from Zoom from their parliamentary office. For many people, making a submission is the only time in their life that they directly engage with Parliament. People travel from all over the country to come here and to make an oral submission, often only for 10 minutes. It is incumbent on us as elected members of Parliament to give them the respect they deserve by being physically present and listening to them in person.
      Similarly, just as a Minister will need to explain why a bill may be skipping select committee entirely, there will now also be a requirement for a Minister to give a reason if they choose to refer a bill to a select committee for less than six months. This is not necessarily to discourage that practice, because there will be cases when it’s needed, but it does put the justification on the record and will help members of the public understand why the Government has made that decision. It is another step towards increasing transparency in the legislative process.
      There were many other changes agreed by the committee, and I’m sure other speakers in this debate will address some of them. These include making the pecuniary interests register clearer and fairer, looking at how select committees can use modern technology such as artificial intelligence to help manage the sometimes overrun submissions process, and further refining scrutiny weeks for the next Parliament. I’m incredibly proud of the work that we have done to make the next Parliament just that bit better, both for elected members but, more importantly, for the members of the public we are here to serve.Dr TRACEY McLELLAN (Labour) (15:17): Thank you, Mr Speaker, on this final sitting day of the 54th Parliament. I want to begin by acknowledging the members of the Standing Orders Committee, and you, Mr Speaker, for chairing that committee; the Clerk of the House, Dr David Wilson; David Bagnall, Principal Clerk; and all of the officials and the specialist advisers that we were afforded the opportunity to have with us, who have worked through this process of this review.
      Now, uncharitably, Standing Orders can sound like the somewhat boring machinery behind Parliament rather than the substance of what Parliament actually does, but they do matter, and they matter enormously. They determine who gets heard; they determine who can object to who gets heard. They determine all sorts of things that happen in this place. It’s about how the Government gets scrutinised. It’s how much opportunity the public has to participate in these processes, and, ultimately, it is determinative of how carefully this House makes law.
      So changes to the rules of Parliament shouldn’t simply be imposed by whichever Government happens to have the numbers, or whichever party happens to have the numbers at any particular time. The committee works on the basis of overwhelming support across parties, because the legitimacy of the rules that make this place work depends on all of us having confidence in those rules.
      The committee has tried to do two things at once—and I agree with many of the points made by the Hon Louise Upston. These are to make Parliament work more effectively while protecting proper scrutiny and democratic participation. The first and probably the most significant proposal is the creation of this new Legislative Scrutiny Committee. The Standing Orders Committee, at least, was trying to deal with what is a very real problem, increasing pressure on House time and on select committees, while still protecting what should be proper scrutiny of legislation. The Parliament has seen a very substantial use of urgency this term. The committee heard directly about the consequences of going through legislation at pace, going through the lawmaking process too quickly, less scrutiny, fewer opportunities for members to influence legislation, less public participation, and legislation sometimes bypassing or receiving a truncated select committee process, which is very important in terms of appropriate consideration.
      The legislative scrutiny committee is an attempt to respond to that very pressure and to do things in a slightly different—or, hopefully, slightly better—way for appropriate, largely non-controversial legislation, of which there is certainly some. It would provide another place for that level of detailed scrutiny to occur. It’s a new place where we could examine legislative quality, consider bills, question Ministers—still in public—and have some cases, undertake a detailed consideration that would otherwise happen in the committee of the whole House stage.
